title: Saudi Arabia intercepts drone, missile as Houthis report attack on Sanaa
excerpt: The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a drone and a missile launched by the Houthis, while the media affiliated with the Yemeni group reported that at least six...
body_text:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a drone and a missile launched by the Houthis, while the media affiliated with the Yemeni group reported that at least six people were wounded in an air attack on an oil company’s fuel station in Sanaa.

The Yemen News Agency quoted the spokesperson for the Ministry of Health and Environment, Anis al-Asbahi, as saying on Sunday that Saudi aircraft targeted a fuel station operated by the state-run oil company on 60th Street, “injuring six employees and causing material damage”.

There was no immediate comment on the claim from the Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

Separately, the Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Turki al-Maliki, said the country’s air defences destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh.

Al-Maliki did not provide further details or report any casualties or damage in his post on X.

His statement came hours after he announced that a ballistic missile was intercepted and destroyed as it targeted the country’s western region, on the coast of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia’s western region has key energy infrastructure, including the Yanbu oil terminal, a facility for crude exports, and the Jazan refinery in the far southwest of the country, which borders Yemen.

The Houthis have attacked oil installations in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, along with airports and military sites.

Meanwhile, clashes continue between the internationally recognised Yemeni government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, amid warnings of worsening displacement and food shortages.

Since seizing Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, and the internationally recognised government has controlled much of the south. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted the fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again this summer when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.

The group then carried out a lightning offensive in September, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline near the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Government forces launched a counteroffensive last month to recapture territory from the Houthis, but forces allied to the government earlier this month said they would withdraw from areas around the strait and focus on defending Aden.

Analysts say the conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics in Yemen, and it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the US-Israel war on Iran.

Houthi attacks have killed 26 people in Saudi Arabia since September, including 23 in strikes on airports, according to the kingdom’s authorities.

On Thursday, a tower housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund in Riyadh’s financial district sustained damage on several floors in a Houthi attack, authorities said.

A skyscraper belonging to state oil giant Aramco was also damaged in a strike at the beginning of the month.

title: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
excerpt: Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports a...
body_text:
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.

The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.

The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan‘s war increasingly relies on drones.

Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.

Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.

A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.

In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.

The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.

The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.

A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.

Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.

Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.

Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.

The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.

Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.

The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.

The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

title: Zelenskyy urges US to release Patriot missiles as Russia kills 3 in Ukraine
excerpt: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged the United States to approve the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles after a week of Russian attacks across 20 regions of the country with the la...
body_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged the United States to approve the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles after a week of Russian attacks across 20 regions of the country with the latest ones killing three near Kyiv and in Zaporizhzhia.

In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russia launched about 2,700 attack drones, nearly 1,460 guided aerial bombs and 165 missiles over the past week. A significant share of the missiles were ballistic, he said, including some supplied by North Korea.

“Against this backdrop, it is particularly difficult to understand the delays in the delivery of antiballistic systems to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine is short of US-made Patriot interceptors, which can shoot down ballistic missiles.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s partners had already paid for the missiles through a NATO-coordinated programme that funds purchases of US weapons for Kyiv. However, their delivery is still awaiting Washington’s approval.

One of the latest Russian attacks hit a five-storey apartment building early on Sunday in the village of Dymer, north of Kyiv, causing part of it to collapse.

Zelenskyy initially said nine people had been evacuated and 14 were unaccounted for.

Rescuers later recovered two bodies as emergency crews searched for 11 people, including two children, who were missing, according to Russia’s Interfax news agency, citing Radio Liberty.

Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the Zaporizhia regional military administration, also said a man was killed in Russian shelling in the city of Zaporizhzhia.

Also on Sunday, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces struck a cargo ship northeast of Ukraine’s Black Sea port city of Odesa overnight.

The ministry said Russian drones struck the Pravoberezhna electricity facility in Zaporizhzhia, which it said supplied power to Ukrainian arms manufacturers. It reported further strikes on an oil refinery, electrical substations and a data centre operated by MKM Telecom.

In its battlefield update, the ministry claimed Russian forces had taken control of the Ukrainian village of Sosnovyi Bir in the northeastern Kharkiv region and destroyed a launcher for Ukraine’s Neptune coastal missile system.

It also said it struck energy and transport facilities it described as serving Ukraine’s military. The Russian claims could not be independently verified.

title: Iran unveils dual-missile launcher, new ‘missile city’: What to know
excerpt: Iran is putting its upgraded missile systems and underground military facilities on display, delivering a defiant message that it still has significant military capabilities despite US-Israeli attacks...
body_text:
Iran is putting its upgraded missile systems and underground military facilities on display, delivering a defiant message that it still has significant military capabilities despite US-Israeli attacks.

The latest showcase included a dual-missile launcher capable of firing two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state media broadcasting footage of military commanders touring an underground missile facility.

Officials insisted Iran has strengthened its missile and air-defence capabilities since previous rounds of fighting, including the launch of the US-Israel war in late February. Still, Iran is under mounting economic pressure from a naval blockade imposed by the United States that has disrupted its oil exports.

Here’s everything to know about the new dual-missile launcher and Iran’s “missile city”:

Iran has developed a range of ballistic and cruise missiles over the past three decades.

The new dual-missile launcher was unveiled as Major-General Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), toured the underground facility on Saturday.

The IRGC aerospace force flaunted its range of upgraded missiles and military equipment, including the launcher, which is designed to carry and fire two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state broadcaster IRIB.

Liquid-fuelled missiles are launched vertically and offer speed-control capabilities, which can aid in overcoming air defence systems, IRIB reported.

State media said the latest generations of Iranian missiles have improved in range, accuracy and guidance capabilities independent of the US Global Positioning System (GPS).

Vahidi’s tour followed the IRGC aerospace force’s announcement of a new underground facility on November 10, according to the semiofficial Tasnim News Agency.

Tasnim said Iran is constructing underground military complexes able to continue weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment.

The IRGC has said it transferred its missile and drone production lines from the surface to underground facilities to allow it continuing missile production.

Footage broadcast by IRIB on Saturday showed kilometres of tunnels and hundreds of missiles and launchers, including double launchers, among other systems.

Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar said it was not clear when the state broadcaster’s footage of the underground site was filmed.

“The IRGC are trying to send a message to the outside world that they are not short of ammunition; they have enough missiles and enough launchers,” he said.

“If the war resumes again, they are going to deploy these capabilities,” he added. “It is a part of their propaganda, but also, Iran is flexing its muscles and trying to restore deterrence.”

Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, said Iran can safely store spare parts, raw materials and chemicals needed for creating missiles and drones at its underground sites in addition to storing finished missiles and drones.

Iran has been planning for such a scenario for decades, he said. “So there’s no doubt that Iran has stored an enormous amount of all of this,” Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, told Al Jazeera.

“They’ve shown … they’re prepared to stand sanctions and keep fighting.”

Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in international security at King’s College London, said Iran is now more emboldened than ever to assert its military capabilities due to the outcome of the US midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered sweeping losses.

The rising cost of living as a result of the war on Iran was a major factor in how people in the US voted in the elections, which saw Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress.

“So [Trump] looks more like the boy who cried wolf,” Pinfold told Al Jazeera. “There seems to be a feeling that the US has been deterred or disincentivised from escalating the conflict.”

Khouri said Iran has taken a gradual approach to showing its technical and military capabilities as well as its political will to strike back.

“[This is] all designed to show the US and Israel … [that] Iran has very sophisticated capabilities that can both evade the Western defence forces and defence systems … and at the same time reach targets that it wants to hit in the countries that it decides to attack,” he said.

At the same time, Iran is suffering under the US naval blockade of its southern ports, so it feels the need to escalate because it feels backed into a corner, Pinfold noted.

He added that Iran’s economy is already in recession and there are growing fears it could suffer an even bigger hit.

“Very little if any oil is coming out of Iran at the moment,” Pinfold said.

Russian ship attacked by drone in Baltic Sea off Finland

A Russian cargo ship caught fire after a suspected Ukrainian drone attack in the Baltic Sea. The vessel was heading to Kaliningrad, but instead drifted into Finnish waters, where Finland authorities imposed temporary air and maritime restrictions as the crew evacuated.

title: Tom Jackson, Broncos' Orange Crush linebacker and ESPN legend, dead at 75
excerpt: Washington Commanders defensive end Deatrich Wise Jr. said players should decide for themselves whether to use riskier celebrations after Detroit Lions star Aidan Hutchinson tore his ACL while celebra...
body_text:
Washington Commanders defensive end Deatrich Wise Jr. said players should decide for themselves whether to use riskier celebrations after Detroit Lions star Aidan Hutchinson tore his ACL while celebrating a sack.

The start of ESPN's "Sunday NFL Countdown" turned into an emotional, tearful announcement from longtime network host Chris Berman that former Denver Broncos linebacker and longtime network analyst Tom Jackson has died.

Jackson died on Friday at the age of 75. No cause of death has been announced.

It was the wishes of the family that the news be delivered on ESPN by Berman.

AL MICHAELS CHOKES UP DURING MOVING TRIBUTE TO DAN HICKS ON THURSDAY NIGHT FOOTBALL – HIS BEST MOMENT IN YEARS

"It was unexpected," Berman said. "He was a vital 75. Tom was poignant. He was active. This is a shock. I saw him just two or three weeks ago. He made a surprise visit to the studio.

"I saw him in September when his daughter, Taylor, was married in their area in Cincinnati. Talk with them at length on Tuesday. We would talk about life. We would talk about the world. You know, eventually, we'd get the football, some conversations, we wouldn't.

FILE PHOTO: Denver Broncos linebacker Tom Jackson chases Cleveland Browns running back Kevin Mack during the 1986 AFC Championship Game at Cleveland Stadium in Cleveland, Ohio, on Jan. 11, 1987. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

"We always talked on the holidays, so Thanksgiving is coming, and Christmas, of course, but it's just... actually unbelievable that on this day, November 22nd, is the day that we always talked, even if it would be a Sunday."

The NFL world will surely react to this in consensus grief.

NFL COACHES SHARE INCREDIBLE MIKE DITKA STORIES AS FOOTBALL WORLD MOURNS THE BEARS LEGEND

To a generation of NFL players, coaches, and fans, Jackson was a fine player. To a different generation he was in their living room in the morning on "Sunday NFL Countdown" and in the evening on the network's NFL highlights show.

"The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history," the Denver Broncos said in a statement.

Linebacker Tom Jackson of the Denver Broncos smiles as he leaves the field after a game against the Buffalo Bills at Rich Stadium on Oct. 21, 1984, in Orchard Park, N.Y. The Broncos defeated the Bills 37-7. (Getty Images)

"An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos’ first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos Country.

"TJ’s dynamic personality, quick wit and football knowledge made him a natural for television and paved the way for a Hall of Fame broadcasting career. For generations of fans, Tom was an iconic fixture on ESPN’s Sunday NFL Countdown and NFL Primetime, sharing his thoughtful insight with an unmistakable sense of humor that defined an era of sports broadcasting.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Above all, TJ loved the Broncos and was a cherished member of our family for more than 50 years. We extend our deepest sympathies to Tom’s wife, Jennifer, his daughters, Taylor and Morgan, and all of his family, friends and teammates."

Thomas Louie "Tom" Jackson was born on April 4, 1951 in Cleveland, Ohio.

ESPN commentator Tom Jackson appears on Monday Night Football on Nov. 13, 2006, as the Carolina Panthers host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Charlotte. The Panthers won 24-10. (Getty Images)

SUPER BOWL CHAMPION CRAIG MORTON’S CAUSE OF DEATH REVEALED AFTER HIS PASSING AT 83

After playing college football at the University of Louisville, he was selected by the Broncos in the fourth round of the 1973 NFL Draft and spent his entire 14-year playing career (1973–1986) as a linebacker in Denver.

A cornerstone of the Broncos' famed "Orange Crush" defense, Jackson earned multiple Pro Bowl and All-Pro selections, was inducted into the Broncos Ring of Fame in 1992.

title: Can we build a more ethical AI future?
excerpt:
Marc Lamont Hill speaks with tech entrepreneur Anil Dash about AI’s risks and the fight for ethical technology.

The artificial intelligence boom is transforming the global economy and concentrating e...
body_text:
Marc Lamont Hill speaks with tech entrepreneur Anil Dash about AI’s risks and the fight for ethical technology.

The artificial intelligence boom is transforming the global economy and concentrating enormous power in the hands of a few technology companies. But a series of developments is raising new questions about the industry’s stability and accountability from the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy to a wave of technology outages affecting the US government, major banks, companies and aviation systems alongside reports of hacked refrigerators across Europe. Concerns are mounting over the economic risks, mass layoffs, privacy and environmental impact of AI. And as AI company Anthropic began trading publicly, reaching a $2 trillion valuation, questions are mounting over whether the extraordinary levels of AI investment are sustainable. Is there a future where AI can be used for the collective good?

This week on UpFront, Marc Lamont Hill speaks with Anil Dash, former adviser to the White House Office of Digital Strategy in former United States President Barack Obama’s administration, about the risks of the AI boom, Silicon Valley’s growing political influence and the urgent need for greater accountability.

title: Netanyahu rival condemns settler arson attacks on Palestinian villages in West Bank
excerpt:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes

Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied...
body_text:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes

Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.

Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes were set alight in the village.

Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars were torched in Deir Abu Mashal.

An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.

“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”

Referring to Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”

Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by President Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the Israeli government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.

In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.

Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.

Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada, and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.

“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”

Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.

Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.

Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

title: 'Crazy': Moderates fear Dem leadership promised far-left reparations and ICE demands in turn of votes
excerpt: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital she hopes to work with President Donald Trump on a stock trading ban and healthcare, while leaving the door open to a potential presidentia...
body_text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital she hopes to work with President Donald Trump on a stock trading ban and healthcare, while leaving the door open to a potential presidential run.

Progressive House Democrats believe party leaders could use their newly won majority to back their far-left agenda on such matters as reparations and abolishing ICE, despite pushback from moderates concerned about the party's direction.

Newly elected Democratic Caucus Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and progressive lawmakers told Fox News Digital that proposals to ICE, expand deportation protections and pursue slavery reparations will be part of the party's legislative discussions under Speaker nominee Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., despite concerns from moderates that the agenda could distract from affordability.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Reps. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla., second from left, Nanette Barragán, D-Calif., and Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., attend the House Democratic Steering and Policy Committee hearing on "Americans impacted by service cuts, mass firings and healthcare price hikes," due to the government shutdown in the Capitol Visitor Center on Wednesday, October 22, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

‘SQUAD’ MEMBER ANNOUNCES ‘MAJORITY PRIORITIES’ INCLUDING REPARATIONS, ABOLISHING ICE AFTER BLUE WAVE

"Jeffries has been very clear, he wants to make sure everyone in the caucus is well represented," Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told Fox News Digital.

Lieu told Fox News Digital that he is "excited" to have "discussions on everything" with members of the caucus, including proposals involving reparations and abolishing ICE.

The California Democrat said he would also be willing to consider other priorities of Rep. Ayanna Presley, D-Mass., including "Medicare for All," "abortion justice" and extending Temporary Protected Status for Third World migrants.

Rep. Ted Lieu speaks during a press conference at the United States Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 3, 2026. (Matt McClain/The Washington Post)

'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., a prominent supporter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), told Fox News Digital that progressives and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries have found common ground on several priorities outlined in Pressley's agenda, including expanding healthcare access and public housing.

"Of course, there are going to be areas where leader Jeffries and DSA are going to be in strong opposition, but there are also areas like expanding Medicaid, public housing, and housing issues in general, where there are shared values that unite everybody," Ocasio-Cortez, a potential 2028 presidential contender, told Fox News Digital.

Ocasio-Cortez has also begun working with Democratic leadership on the House Energy and Commerce Committee to advance her healthcare priorities, a senior congressional democratic staffer told Fox News Digital.

However, moderate Democrats were skeptical that party leadership would embrace the progressive agenda, with some questioning whether Jeffries and other leaders had promised to consider those demands in exchange for support during the leadership elections.

"Our agenda is to focus on costs," Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital. "What's clear is we had an overwhelming majority. I think some of my colleagues seem to be unhappy with winning in a place we've never won before."

Gottheimer accused progressive colleagues of wanting to "squawk and complain and make their demands" rather than focus on the issues that helped Democrats win the midterm elections.

The New Jersey Democrat also rejected proposals to "defund police, have open borders, or get rid of the United States Senate," arguing that neither he nor Democratic leadership would support such policies.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'

Rep. Ayanna Pressley takes to the stage at an Election Night party for Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll on Nov. 3, 2026. (Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

Gottheimer, an outspoken critic of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), suggested that Pressley's priorities more closely resemble the organization's platform than the broader Democratic Party's agenda.

"The DSA, they have their own agenda," Gottheimer said.

RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY

Another Democratic lawmaker, who requested anonymity, told Fox News Digital that they and a longtime colleague viewed the prospect of leadership adopting the progressive agenda as "crazy."

The lawmaker also speculated that Lieu and Jeffries were expressing openness to progressive proposals to avoid opposition during Wednesday's leadership elections.

Jeffries and Pressley did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

title: Rivals author Jilly Cooper accused of ‘extensive and deliberate plagiarism’
excerpt:
Analysis reportedly finds striking similarities in dialogue and narrative structure between late author’s novel, Prudence, and two of her contemporaries

Jilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising ...
body_text:
Analysis reportedly finds striking similarities in dialogue and narrative structure between late author’s novel, Prudence, and two of her contemporaries

Jilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists.

The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and The Franchise Affair by Josephine Tey.

According to a report in the Observer, Cooper, who died last October, committed “what appears to be extensive and deliberate plagiarism” by lifting at least 35 passages from The Serial alone.

McFadden’s daughter, Caroline McFadden, told the publication: “To steal her work so extensively and to profit off it is unconscionable.”

She said she was considering legal action, saying: “It absolutely boils my blood to think of someone stealing my mother’s work because I know how hard she worked at her craft.

“I will be looking at legal options as this can’t be allowed to stand. I sincerely hope that all of Dame Cooper’s work will be scrutinised to see if this was a pattern of hers and other talented authors’ work stolen.”

Cooper, who has sold more than 11m copies of her books in the UK alone, was given a damehood in the 2024 new year honours list for her services to literature and charity.

Disney+ is currently airing the second series of Rivals, the award-winning television adaptation of her most famous work. The show combines TV industry intrigue and racy sex scenes against the backdrop of the Cotswolds countryside in the fictional guise of Rutshire.

In its investigation, the Observer detailed 15 allegedly plagiarised passages from The Serial, which was first published from late 1975 as a weekly serialisation in a US newspaper before it was released as a book in May 1977.

In The Serial, McFadden, who died in 2024, created the off-and-on-again couple Kate and Harvey Holroyd, two progressives in California’s Marin County. The Observer noted several similarities with the dialogue in Cooper’s character, Berenice, an American feminist.

In The Serial, Kate says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open, loving relationship, based on growth and trust and sharing, and Harvey wanted his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we just weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

In Prudence, Berenice says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open living relationship based on trust and growth, and all he wanted was his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

The publication also cited another example from The Serial in which Harvey was offered lifestyle advice. The passage said: “Cut out the nine-to-five shit, Harv. You gotta get in touch with the universe. That’s the first step.”

In Prudence, Berenice offered similar advice. “You ought to cut out that nine to five shit … And get in touch with the universe.”

The Observer said it began looking at Prudence after a reader pointed out similarities with a scene in Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair.

The publication alleged that Cooper “lifts directly” from chapter 22 of the novel “both in narrative architecture and in line-by-line choice of words”. Tey died in 1952 and left no heirs.

Cooper is said to have praised The Serial for its parody of the modern feminist in a 1982 Mail on Sunday column. She said she was “tremendously comforted” when she “came across a passage in the novel The Serial by Cyra McFadden, a marvellously funny send-up of American trendies in the late seventies”.

An inquest held last year concluded that Cooper suffered a fatal head injury in a fall at her Gloucestershire home. She was found by family on 4 October 2025 and died in hospital the following day.

The Guardian has contacted Cooper’s agent, Felicity Blunt at Curtis Brown, and her publisher, Penguin, for comment. The Observer said both had declined to provide a comment.

Daniel Jones was released by the Indianapolis Colts following their 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask what’s going on with the Colts, and if Puka Nacua’s surgery means that the Los Angeles Rams will miss the playoffs.

The Indianapolis Colts walked away from starting quarterback Daniel Jones on Friday to the surprise of some, including Jones himself, because only two weeks earlier the club spurned a trade offer by the Baltimore Ravens and promised Jones he would remain their quarterback.

Those new details from one of the more curious personnel juggling episodes by an NFL team recently is evidence the Colts do not have their act fully together.

Jones was expecting to remain with the Colts for the remainder of the regular season and was surprised that would no longer be the case when he was told of his release on Friday, a source told OutKick.

DANIEL JONES, JONATHAN TAYLOR REACT TO COLTS FIRE SALE AS THEY REMAIN PUT: 'YOU'RE NOT HAPPY TO SEE IT'

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) leaves the field after an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, Sept. 7, 2025, in Indianapolis. (AP Photo/AJ Mast)

But the quarterback was indeed released and now must wait until Monday to see if he is claimed, which will decide a new team for him, or clears waivers which will allow him to make a decision on what team he joins and when.

If Jones clears waivers, a source said he and his representatives will study the landscape to see if a team that is in the playoff hunt or likely headed to the playoffs needs him as either a backup or a replacement for an injured starter.

Jones and his reps didn't think it would come to this.

Before the trade deadline on Nov. 10, the Colts told Jones he was staying with the team because he was not being traded. That didn't mean there wasn't interest.

MORE PROOF THAT ANY TEAM TRADING FOR DANIEL JONES AT THE NFL TRADE DEADLINE IS CHASING FOOL'S GOLD

Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones throws before a National Football League game against the Las Vegas Raiders in Indianapolis, Indiana, on Oct. 5, 2025. (AJ Mast/AP Photo)

As OutKick reported in the lead-up to the trade deadline, Jones was the subject of trade talks. And over the weekend it was confirmed that the Ravens not only showed interest in Jones but made an offer for him.

The offer: A 2027 fourth-round pick for Jones and a 2027 fifth-round pick, as first reported by ESPN.

COLTS HAD JONATHAN TAYLOR AND GROVER STEWART TRADE OFFERS BUT DIDN'T COMPLETE DEALS THAT EVENTUALLY GOT PULLED

The Colts, however, turned down the offer.

This was the same Colts that when all was done after the trade deadline, had traded offensive lineman Quenton Nelson, and receivers Josh Downs and Keenan Allen. So, the Colts kept their quarterback while choosing to strip away talent around him.

The Colts privately said just after the deadline the issue with not trading Jones then was they weren't being offered good value in return.

This, of course, seems a ridiculous stance now.

Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) hands off to Jonathan Taylor (28) during the first half of a preseason NFL football game against the Green Bay Packers, Saturday, Aug. 16, 2025, in Indianapolis. (AP Photo/AJ Mast)

Firstly, the offer by the Ravens was not necessarily a final offer, according to a league source. There were days remaining before the trade deadline, including a weekend of games, before those two teams ended their talks about Jones.

And, indeed, the Ravens made a trade for Arizona quarterback Jacoby Brissett as a fallback to getting Jones. The deal they made with the Cardinals was better than the one they offered the Colts because the Cardinals continued to negotiate with Baltimore about a deal.

The Ravens eventually gave up a 2027 fourth-round pick for Brissett and a 2028 seventh-rounder in return.

But the greater point is the Colts, 10 days after the trade deadline, after telling Jones he was staying, and declining an offer to trade him because it was deemed not good enough, then cut Jones.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones runs off the field following an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders in Indianapolis, Indiana, on Oct. 5, 2025. (AJ Mast/AP Photo)

It is in fact worse than zero because a trade would have sent Jones and his current year base salary obligations to the Ravens. Waiving him leaves Indianapolis paying his remaining base salary if he goes unclaimed, as expected.

And, of course, if the Colts thought getting a fourth-rounder for Jones was unacceptable 10 days ago, now they are without Jones and don't get that fourth-rounder in return in next April's draft.

The Colts have been the subject of talk among NFL executives for a couple of weeks. And, as it was prior to the trade deadline, that discussion is not flattering.

title: Remembering Fiona: Timeline of how the hippo beat the odds, became a star and inspired millions
excerpt: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's beloved 9-year-old Nile hippo, died after ingesting a visitor's knitted hat that was deflected into her habitat by a ceiling fan. She was born premature at 29 pounds, Fiona...
body_text:
Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's beloved 9-year-old Nile hippo, died after ingesting a visitor's knitted hat that was deflected into her habitat by a ceiling fan. She was born premature at 29 pounds, Fiona overcame steep odds to become a global sensation.

Millions of Americans are mourning the loss of Fiona.

The 9-year-old Nile hippo who captured the hearts of people all over the country after surviving an early birth in January 2017 and becoming the world's first premature hippo to be raised by humans died at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden on Thursday, Nov. 19, after ingesting a visitor's knitted hat that was accidentally deflected into her enclosure.

Born six weeks early at just 29 pounds, Fiona rapidly drew enthusiastic online followers. She also helped push annual attendance at the zoo as fans traveled from far and wide to catch a glimpse of the spunky creature.

Her death occurred roughly a decade after another high-profile demise at the same zoo, when Harambe, a 17-year-old western lowland gorilla, was fatally shot by zoo staff in May 2016 after a young boy climbed into his enclosure.

BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT

The Cincinnati Zoo on Friday released new autopsy findings after Fiona's death.

A postmortem examination determined that a foreign object, confirmed to be a hat that zoo officials said accidentally wound up in her enclosure, was lodged deep inside the hippo's massive digestive tract, according to the zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger.

During Fiona's early weeks of life, Cincinnati Zoo staff provided 24/7 critical care to keep the hippo warm and fed until she grew strong enough to thrive. (Cincinnati Zoo)

The hat was lodged halfway through her small intestine, roughly 25 feet past her stomach and still 50 feet from exiting her body.

Zoo visitors, local and federal leaders, and fans all around the world are still trying to absorb news of the animal's passing.

"I was really mad," a young woman in downtown Cincinnati told Fox News Digital on Friday. "I know it was a fluke accident … but it just seemed like it could have been prevented in some way. And she was just so iconic. This is just devastating to the community."

Fiona came into the world under extraordinary circumstances.

The woman added, "I was really upset. I went home from work after that."

Fiona has had books written about her, murals painted of her and even clothing with cute depictions of her created in her honor. The city of Cincinnati has considered her its unofficial mascot.

Fiona came into the world on Jan. 24, 2017, under extraordinary circumstances.

The hippo was born six weeks before she was due. She "was too small to stand and nurse from her mom, Bibi," according to the Cincinnati Zoo.

She weighed a mere 29 pounds at birth — 25 pounds lighter than the lowest recorded birth weight for Nile hippos, according to the zoo.

Born six weeks premature in January 2017, Fiona weighed just 29 pounds at birth — 25 pounds lighter than the lowest recorded birth weight for Nile hippos. Zoo staff worked around the clock to help her survive.  (Cincinnati Zoo)

"The zoo's care team had to step in and figure out how to feed her, what to feed her, how to keep her warm, and how to manage critical care 24/7 while juggling other daily responsibilities," the zoo's website states.

"It took a village, but #TeamFiona did it!"

Fiona's father, Henry, was 35 years old when she was born (he died in Oct. 2017). Bibi was 17. Fiona was the first Nile hippo to be born at the Cincinnati Zoo in over 50 years.

Fiona experienced a big year of growth in 2018.

LOCH NESS MONSTER SIGHTINGS JUMP IN 2026 AS SCIENTIST DRILLS INTO LEGENDARY MYSTERY

By her first birthday, Jan. 24, 2018, she tipped the scales at 650 pounds.

She also attracted a lot of attention during this period.

Fiona the hippo "became a beloved symbol of hope and a source of inspiration for millions of people," the zoo said.  (Cincinnati Zoo)

"By sharing her ups and downs with the world (every day for almost two years), she became a beloved symbol of hope and a source of inspiration for millions of people," the zoo's website states.

By her third birthday in Jan. 2019, she weighed half a ton — with zoo officials describing her as a "thousand-pound toddler."

Fiona's half-brother, Fritz, was born to Bibi on Aug. 3, 2022, fathered by a male named Tucker.

BABY ELEPHANT MAKES HISTORIC ARRIVAL AT SMITHSONIAN'S NATIONAL ZOO AS FIRST BIRTH IN NEARLY 25 YEARS

The zoo documented when Fiona and baby Fritz first met three weeks later.

"Five-year-old Fiona was curious but took her cues from her mom, Bibi, and backed off when Fritz got almost close enough for a nose boop," the zoo said.

Fiona helped push annual attendance at the Cincinnati Zoo past 1.7 million visitors as fans traveled from across the country to see her in the zoo's Hippo Cove attraction. (Cincinnati Zoo)

"This first intro went very well. Bibi was appropriately protective of Fritz but was not aggressive toward Fiona," the Cincinnati Zoo's animal care director, Christina Gorsuch, said at the time.

"The exposure was brief but a great first step."

At the beginning of 2025, Fiona celebrated her eighth birthday.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, a Cincinnati man said on Friday, "She wasn’t supposed to be here to begin with. The fact that she overcame so much … it was always inspiring. And to see her with her family, you know, mom, dad, half-brother — it was always nice to see."

Reflecting on the hippo's early life, Cincinnati Zoo marketing manager Amy LaBarbara said that she was an instant social media hit.

Fiona the Nile hippo attracted scores of visitors to the Cincinnati Zoo, where she lived with other hippos, including her mother Bibi and her half-brother Fritz. Books have been written about her and murals painted in her honor. (Cincinnati Zoo)

"We shared updates on Fiona on social media every day during the first year of her life, and people couldn’t get enough," LaBarbara said at the time.

"We even tried to stop at one point but got so much pushback that we kept up with the daily posts."

LaBarbara said that "posts about Fiona and her little brother Fritz consistently [got] millions of views and likes from a global audience."

On Thursday, Nov. 19, Cincinnati Zoo officials announced that Fiona had died after a visitor's hat was tossed in the air and a ceiling fan deflected it over the hippo enclosure's viewing glass.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week," the statement read.

"Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome," officials added.

Fiona is shown eying her specialty birthday cake, later enjoying it in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo on Jan. 23, 2020 in Cincinnati. (AP Photo/John Minchillo)

The zoo said Fiona's team "performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover."

Second lady Usha Vance, a mother of four, paid a heartbreaking tribute to Fiona after the hippo died.

Vance shared a touching family photo of one of her children visiting Fiona as she mourned the death of the world-famous hippo.

"We are so sad," she wrote in part on Instagram.

"We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona. Our family loved visiting her at the @cincinnatizoo," second lady Usha Vance wrote on Instagram next to a photo of one of her children interacting with the hippo. (Usha Vance)

Fiona would have been 10 years old in Jan. 2027.

"In those 10 years, she inspired millions with her story of survival and did so much to raise awareness and caring for her species," the zoo said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Zoo officials have asked the public to "keep the people who worked with Fiona and tried to save her in your thoughts and prayers."

"They loved her and did their best to save her," the statement added.

Fiona happily smashed her birthday cake on Jan. 23, 2020, in Cincinnati. (AP Photo/John Minchillo)

"They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time."

Gorsuch, the director of animal care, said Fritz and the zoo's other hippos, Bibi and Tucker, have been eating and behaving normally since Fiona's death.

The area around the Hippo Cove was to be closed throughout the weekend. The animal care team were "shaken and trying to navigate this loss," the zoo said.

"We come here every Saturday morning," a dad in Cincinnati told Fox News Digital on Friday about the zoo. "We grew up with Fiona. Our two kids — we have a membership here. And [Fiona] was always a staple of why we came over."

Melissa Rudy, Louis Casiano and Bonny Chu, all of Fox News Digital, contributed reporting.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: The Drugs Don’t Work
excerpt:
A look at how antibiotic overuse could fuel superbugs, killing eight million people annually by 2050.

The challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance show where its impact is most acutely and tragic...
body_text:
A look at how antibiotic overuse could fuel superbugs, killing eight million people annually by 2050.

The challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance show where its impact is most acutely and tragically manifested: infant mortality in the developing world, specifically in sub-Saharan Africa. This film shows what these bland statistics mean in real terms to the health workers and families affected, following them as they struggle to fight this battle with low-tech solutions.

The Drugs Don’t Work follows the battle to the United Kingdom and examines how and why penicillin, the world’s most successful antibiotic, was invented. It then examines why pharmaceutical companies like GlaxoSmithKline are struggling to produce novel solutions to the problem of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

The film also explores the cutting edge of academic research at British universities and hospitals supported by the power of the UK-based tech company DeepMind, and features academics and advocates who are devoting their lives to solving the problem. Returning to Africa, it shows how local innovation and the tools offered by the developed world are now saving lives and contributing to the global battle against AMR – an effort that could ultimately save millions of lives.

title: Indiana's national championship defense on the brink after overtime upset to Washington
excerpt: Done tolerating the constant disrespect aimed at the Hoosiers, Cignetti went scorched earth during his weekly press conference, taking aim at the College Football Playoff committee, schedule critics, ...
body_text:
Done tolerating the constant disrespect aimed at the Hoosiers, Cignetti went scorched earth during his weekly press conference, taking aim at the College Football Playoff committee, schedule critics, and anyone minimizing Indiana’s achievements, while declaring his team "ripped the heart out" of Ohio State.

The reigning national champions may not even get into the dance this year.

Unranked Washington (7-4) upset No. 8 Indiana (9-2) 27-24 in overtime on Saturday at Husky Stadium, delivering a significant blow to the Hoosiers' College Football Playoff hopes. Despite holding two fourth-quarter leads, the Hoosiers could not hang on.

title: Displaced Palestinians protest as Israeli air strikes continue in Gaza
excerpt:
Hundreds of displaced Palestinians have protested as Israeli forces continue to destroy residential buildings in Gaza, beyond the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire.

Al Jazeera journal...
body_text:
Hundreds of displaced Palestinians have protested as Israeli forces continue to destroy residential buildings in Gaza, beyond the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire.

Al Jazeera journalist Moath al-Kahlout, reporting from Gaza’s Deir el-Balah, said displaced Palestinians who live in the area near the “Yellow Line” gathered on Saturday to demonstrate against Israel’s intensifying air strikes.

The “Yellow Line” separates Israeli- and Hamas-controlled areas in Gaza since the “ceasefire” signed in October 2025.

“More than 500 housing units have been destroyed in less than a month,” said Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir-el Balah’s Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera.

“This is part of what appears to be a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement aimed at forcing residents out of their camp and destroying as many homes as possible,” Musleh said.

Gaza’s Ministry of Public Works and Housing says 350,000 families are homeless after Israeli attacks destroyed 80 percent of the enclave’s homes.

Meanwhile, flooding in recent weeks devastated temporary tent housing, the ministry said.

The original “Yellow Line”, established under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, marked the area to which Israeli forces initially withdrew. They were expected to make further withdrawals gradually, but instead seized more territory.

“If we go back to October 2025, when the ceasefire was signed, the ‘Yellow Line’ was much further east,” al-Kahlout said.

Now, nearly two-thirds of Gaza is under Israeli army control or subject to access restrictions.

Israeli attacks killed at least four Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday, including three who died when an Israeli drone struck a van delivering food aid to displaced people in Gaza City.

In the past 48 hours, Israeli strikes killed at least nine people, taking the death toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,661, according to the latest report from Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

The ministry said 55 Palestinians were wounded in the past 48 hours, putting the total number of the wounded since October 2025 at 6,062.

Gaza’s Civil Defence said on Saturday that its crew members recovered the bodies and remains of 129 people from 39 homes and other Israeli-destroyed buildings in the Nuseirat refugee camp, az-Zawayda and Deir el-Balah in central Gaza.

Rami al-Aidi, Civil Defence director in central Gaza, said 233 people had been reported missing beneath the rubble of those buildings.

The 53-day operation marked the conclusion of the second phase of a recovery project in central Gaza funded by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Gaza’s Civil Defence said in October that about 8,000 bodies remained under the rubble across the enclave, including about 4,000 in Israeli-controlled areas. The agency warned that recovery could take eight to 10 years with the equipment available.
