title: Dutch defense-industry plan targets 40% growth, €15 billion revenue by 2030
excerpt: PARIS — The Netherlands presented a defense-industrial plan with a target to grow its defense technological and industrial base by 40% by 2030, with local defense industry revenue reaching around €15 ...
body_text:
PARIS — The Netherlands presented a defense-industrial plan with a target to grow its defense technological and industrial base by 40% by 2030, with local defense industry revenue reaching around €15 billion ($16.5 billion).

The government has earmarked €1.6 billion for the industry plan, with a focus on integrated air and missile defense, data-driven command and digital resilience, unmanned and autonomous systems; and military sustainment.

The Netherlands is the seventh-biggest defense spender among European NATO countries, ahead of Sweden, based on data from the alliance, yet the country lacks major defense prime comparable to Sweden’s Saab, Germany’s Rheinmetall or the United Kingdom’s BAE Systems.

Still, the nation of 18 million punches above its weight in several defense technology areas. For example, France’s Thales has a large part of its radar business in the Netherlands, while the country is also home to Destinus, a defense technology company which said this week its Ruta cruise missiles were used by Ukraine to target the Kerch Strait bridge.

“Through this national program, the government, together with industry and research institutions, is rolling up its sleeves to ensure that the armed forces get what they need, both now and in a conflict situation,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.

Warfighting is fundamentally changing, and the impact of technology is “enormous,” the government said, citing space technology, the electromagnetic spectrum, artificial intelligence, cyber, drones and long-range weapons. At the same time, the war in Ukraine has shown the importance of mass, production capability, stocks and the ability to sustain the fight, according to the government.

Strengthening the Dutch defense industry will strengthen the warfighting ability of the Dutch armed forces, according to the government. Spending on the plan will include €600 million for industrial ecosystems and scaling production, €320 million to help pay for international cooperation, and €150 million on make supply chains more resilient.

The Netherlands is counting on the domestic share of Dutch defense-industry revenue to grow faster than the industry’s overall revenue, climbing 50% by 2030 to more than €10 billion. Meanwhile, the target is for exports to grow by about 25%.

The MoD will give greater weight to the origin of products and suppliers in procurement decisions in 2027, and introduce procurement guidelines from the first quarter of 2028 that take into account the origin of raw materials and components, as well a supply-chain transparency, the government said.

The Netherlands is betting on international cooperation in the focus areas, and will actively contribute to leading groups for joint capability development with like-minded partners including Belgium, Germany, France, the U.K. and the Nordic countries, the government said.

“Thanks to their innovative capacity, the Dutch defense industry and research institutions are in a good position to play key roles in global value chains and in this way help reduce risky strategic dependencies for the Netherlands and Europe,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.

To improve financing access for defense firms, the Ministry of Defence together with Invest-NL will set up a €200 million investment fund for dual-use companies in defense and security.

The MoD will also set up the National Institute for Defence Technology, or NIDT, in 2028, with a budget that will climb to €350 million a year by 2030, the government said. The goal of the new institute will be to accelerate innovation and scaling up.

The government plans to strengthen protections against unwanted takeovers and investments in strategically important Dutch defense companies, as well as against leaks of sensitive technology and expertise, with a target to have additional legal instruments in place from 2028.

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

title: ‘Weak and dizzy’: hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal – and what made him crack
excerpt:
Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike

The text message that came from inside the Immigration an...
body_text:
Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike

The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.

The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Pérez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez said.

“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas, are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” the DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. The DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is probably higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it was a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”

Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Pérez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

Cora Pérez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Pérez observed.

“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. The DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Pérez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Pérez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Pérez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”

In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.

“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Pérez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.

“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

Cora Pérez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On 30 October, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Pérez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Pérez. Cora Pérez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”

Cora Pérez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.

“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Pérez about the DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.

Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.

“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.

As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
excerpt:
FDD AI Research Fellow Leah Siskind discusses Google’s warning about hackers leveraging advanced AI to scan software updates and more, on ‘America Reports.’

One of the biggest court battles over arti...
body_text:
FDD AI Research Fellow Leah Siskind discusses Google’s warning about hackers leveraging advanced AI to scan software updates and more, on ‘America Reports.’

One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaks at the opening ceremony of ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Nov. 2, 2026, as ADNOC, OpenAI and G42 announced a major partnership to bring artificial intelligence into the energy industry. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

Coke Morgan Stewart is president and CEO of the Council for Innovation Promotion and the former deputy under secretary of Commerce for intellectual property and deputy director of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.

title: Joanne Young’s faith in the justice system is a sign of real changes, but the courts are still catching up
excerpt:
Years of reforms by prosecutors and police guided the approach that saw Young’s abusers convicted, though much more remains to be done

Hope can be found in the darkest of places. Joanne Young stood o...
body_text:
Years of reforms by prosecutors and police guided the approach that saw Young’s abusers convicted, though much more remains to be done

Hope can be found in the darkest of places. Joanne Young stood outside Winchester crown court on Thursday and said she was relieved – not just for herself and her family – but for women in the future.

Young, who was subjected to years of drugging and rape by her husband, who invited other men to assault her, waived her anonymity to speak out.

She said she hoped her case meant those who had experienced similar abuse could have more faith in the criminal justice system, and that all women and girls who had been abused by men would hear the message that they could be believed and understood.

Given the powerful dignity of Young’s address, it was easy to miss the significance of another remarkable statement, made on the same day by a prosecutor in the case.

“By building the case with a suspect-centric approach, we could prove to a jury that Philip Young could not provide consent on the victim’s behalf and each defendant played a part in this horrific sexual abuse,” said James Foster, a specialist prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service’s Wessex complex casework unit.

Suspect-centric. The fact that a criminal investigation and prosecution is focused on the suspect of the crime should, of course, be unremarkable. But, until quite recently, in cases of rape, sexual assault and domestic abuse, that was rarely the case.

There are some signs, some small green shoots of optimism, that suggest the lumbering criminal justice system is moving in the right direction. Those words from a regional prosecutor indicate a shift that was unimaginable a decade ago, and for people who have spent their lives trying to reform the criminal justice system, it is a sign that change is possible.

In 2018 the Guardian ran a series of stories about a sharp drop in the number of cases that CPS prosecutors were willing to take to trial, prompting concerns about the de facto decriminalisation of rape. Prosecutions fell 60% from 5,190 in 2016-17 to 2,102 in 2019-20, even as the number of incidents reported to police increased.

At a time when the issue was getting little coverage, the Guardian revealed how the CPS held training events for prosecutors, advising they “take the weak cases out of the system” to boost the conviction rate.

In March 2019, Theresa May’s government launched a landmark review into rape investigations. When it reported in 2021, the conclusion was stark: victims were not only being let down, but made to feel like they were the ones under investigation.

The Conservative administration - which had inflicted budget cuts resulting in a 30% reduction in CPS staff and the loss of around 20,000 police officers – issued an unusually frank mea culpa. The policing and crime minister at the time, Kit Malthouse, said “it simply has not been good enough”. The then justice secretary, Robert Buckland, said he was “deeply sorry”.

The response to the review was radical. The Home Office funded Operation Soteria Bluestone, under the leadership of academics and criminology experts Betsy Stanko and Katrin Hohl, to review a number of forces’ cases and unflinchingly reveal their failures.

Police officers and prosecutors were told to change in six key areas by focusing investigations on suspects, disrupting repeat offenders and engaging with victims, and by improving learning and development, officer wellbeing and use of data and digital forensics.

They were also told to stop indiscriminately trawling victims’ personal data, and instead request only information that was relevant and proportionate.

It is clear that in many forces, things have changed – pushed and encouraged by Sarah Crew, the clear-eyed police lead for rape in England and Wales, a role newly created in 2021. Police referrals and CPS charges for rape were back up to 2016 levels by 2024, with the change hailed by independent sexual violence advisers such as Rape Crisis England & Wales.

Nevertheless, charities have continued to warn against complacency: despite the recovery, around 97% of reported rapes never make it to court.

Fears have also been raised that process of change could stall. The courts backlog means rape survivors and complainants are waiting an average of 423 days for trial, with many waiting far longer.

Experts argue that the use of rape myths is still prevalent in courts, noting that during the trial of Russell Brand – which saw the celebrity sentenced to more than 10 years in prison after he was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others – his barrister, Ian Winter, said Brand’s accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Hohl, now the government’s independent advisor on rape, worries that as the police and the CPS move in the right direction, the courts system is being left behind. Last month, she published a report suggesting sexual assault cases prepared under the improved standards come up against a “cliff edge” once they get to trial.

Despite the horror of her experience, Joanne Young has shown us a chink of light in a criminal justice system that has failed too many victims for too long. But the work to fully transform it fully is far from complete.

title: Cybersecurity operation thwarts attack on UK supermarket fridges and freezers
excerpt:
News of operation comes after supermarkets in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks

A secret government cybersecurity operation recently thwarted a cyber-attack on fridges and freeze...
body_text:
News of operation comes after supermarkets in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks

A secret government cybersecurity operation recently thwarted a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged.

The attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable.

News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, comes after supermarket chains in at least seven European countries were affected by a cyber-attack this month.

Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran. The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August.

Experts told the Guardian that, if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM).

“Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could potentially have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe,” he said.

After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cyber-security consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM.

“We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix,” said Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, Ken Munro. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.”

Munro was fortunately attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence.

That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said.

He added that Pen Test Partners also tried to alert the owners of exposed devices. “Some controllers were easy to identify and thus contact the owners, but many thousands at small stores are still exposed,” he said.

“The vulnerability is not easy to find for a number of reasons, but once the method is known, it’s easy to recreate. We have not published that method, so there is still time for small operators to take their controllers off the public internet and/or apply the updated firmware.”

A National Cyber Security Centre spokesperson said it “shared important insight and security advice to ensure that organisations understood potential risks to their networks, and were taking the appropriate measures to mitigate them”.

RDM did not respond to a request for comment. Its chief executive, Ged Evans, told the BBC the vulnerability was “identified in a test environment” that “went beyond” what such exercises usually involved, as it “included dismantling our hardware”.

“In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps,” he said.

title: Darius Rucker says he used to drink a bottle of whiskey a day during wild Hootie & the Blowfish years
excerpt:
Hootie & The Blowfish singer Darius Rucker dedicated new record to mother Carolyn.

Darius Rucker's meteoric rise to fame as the lead singer of Hootie & The Blowfish was captured in the latest Hulu do...
body_text:
Hootie & The Blowfish singer Darius Rucker dedicated new record to mother Carolyn.

Darius Rucker's meteoric rise to fame as the lead singer of Hootie & The Blowfish was captured in the latest Hulu documentary, "They Called Me Hootie."

Breaking onto the scene in the early '90s, the group of college friends from South Carolina broke records with "Cracked Rear View" released in 1994, but fame and fortune came at a cost and Rucker soon spiraled into substance abuse and drinking issues at the peak of the band's popularity.

Rucker, 60, admitted that at one point he was drinking one bottle of whiskey per day while on the road, and casual drug use became routine.

BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG

Darius Rucker was once depending on drugs and alcohol while touring with Hootie & The Blowfish. (Terry Wyatt/WireImage)

"I smoked a little pot," Rucker said. "If we had a day over, someone would get some acid." After the band upgraded to a tour bus, things took a drastic detour.

"One day, I came back to our bus, I walked in the back and two of the guys were lining up some cocaine," Rucker said. "And the party just was on from that point."

‘BACK TO THE FUTURE’ STAR CHRISTOPHER LLOYD CONFESSES HE WAS ‘HOOKED’ ON COCAINE DURING ‘TAXI’ YEARS

He added, "We earned our reputation. We went crazy, man. It was rock and roll."

Rucker recalled once buying trash bags full of mushrooms from someone on the bus.

"I'm like, 'Mushrooms? Really? How many mushrooms you got?' 'We've got two garbage bags of mushrooms,'" he said. "And he's like, 'Well, we're probably gonna make about $45,000.' It’s like, 'What if we give you [$30,000] right now?'

"I went and got T-shirt money and came back with two garbage bags that we kept in our freezers for two and a half years. I always said we never had a drug problem because we could always afford it."

Hootie & the Blowfish found massive success from their debut album, "Cracked Rear View." (Gie Knaeps)

Hootie & the Blowfish supported Darius Rucker at his star unveiling. (Kevin Winter)

Rucker became "instant friends" with Woody Harrelson after meeting backstage following a show, and the pair soon became smoking buddies. Harrelson guessed they had "maybe smoked about 100,000 joints together."

"What do you do when you smoke joints? You just sit and talk. I just loved listening to him spin a yarn," Harrelson said.

COUNTRY SINGER RUSTON KELLY COMMITS TO SOBRIETY AFTER RELAPSING ON DRUGS FOLLOWING FREAK GOLF CART CRASH

At one point, bandmate Mark Bryan remembered when Rucker's penchant for rock 'n' roll impacted the band after he took ecstasy before a gig in London.

"He decided to, like, start exploring the theater during the show," Bryan said. "It felt to me like we were losing the crowd, which is the worst feeling at any time at any show. He probably didn’t feel that way. He probably thought he was taking things to the next level. "

Rucker admitted a girl at the show gave him the drugs, but didn't know why he took it, and said he "could've waited till the show was over, but, you know, I just took it."

Darius Rucker and Woody Harrelson became friends after meeting backstage following a Hootie & the Blowfish show. (KMazur)

"We went on the stage and I was introducing songs we weren’t playing," Rucker said before Bryan explained they had a "huge fight" backstage.

"I headbutted a cinderblock wall," he said. "I’ll never forget doing that. We were not on the same page in that moment."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

While Rucker's life on the road was bumpy, his wife back home was having an equally difficult time with Rucker's touring habits.

"She said that I could straighten up and we would be happy, or I could keep living that life and she'll figure out how she can make me miserable," Rucker recalled.

Hootie & the Blowfish toured in support of the 30th anniversary of "Cracked Rearview Mirror" in 2024. (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images)

"The day before she said that was the last day I partied like that. The next day I called and said I need my own bus."

While taking a break from the band, Rucker visited Harrelson's Hawaiian home, where the singer had the "two best weeks" of his life before tragedy nearly struck.

"We had a blast. We did naked yoga, and I ate so pure and vegan," Rucker remembered.

While walking on the cliffs one day, Harrelson asked if Rucker could swim, and told him if he jumped in, he'd have to navigate a strong rip current.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I dive out, and I open my eyes and look both ways, and I realize, there's no beach and all I see is fish," Rucker said. "And I come up and I start to swim out and I'm caught."

Harrelson admitted the water was "a little rugged that day and he probably shouldn't have gone in."

The members of Hootie & The Blowfish met in college in South Carolina. (Paul Natkin)

"It seemed like forever that we were out there trying to get out," Rucker remembered. "I had gotten myself to a peace. I had accepted that God had given me this amazing life that is exactly what I asked for, and if it had to end right there, then when I got to heaven I was going to say thank you."

"He looked at me, and it was just like Woody from 'Cheers,' he looked at me and giggled and said ‘not on my watch.’"

"I wasn't going to let that happen," Harrelson said before Rucker chimed in that it was "surreal. Woody Harrelson had really literally just saved my life."

The band celebrated the 30th anniversary of their massively successful album "Cracked Rear View" in 2024.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

With tracks including "Only Wanna Be With You," "Hold My Hand" and "Let Her Cry," the debut catalog for the band from South Carolina was released in July 1994 and has been certified platinum 21 times over.

Rucker has two children with his ex-wife, Beth Leonard, and one daughter with Elizabeth Ann Phillips. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

Hootie & the Blowfish went on to release four more studio albums before going on hiatus in 2008, leading Rucker to pursue an entirely different genre: country music.

In 2023, Rucker released his eighth solo album, "Carolyn's Boy," a tribute to his late mother who died in 1992 just as Hootie was picking up steam.

Rucker noted that his biggest disappointment was that his mother never got a chance to see his success.

"At first it was really hard to accept, I mean it was so out of the blue," he said of his mother's death.

"To know that she didn't get to see me do what I told her I was going to do since I was five-years-old. She never got to sit on the phone talking to her girlfriends about me being on David Letterman tonight and how she was going to stay up even though she had to work early tomorrow ... and how she never got to do that is still heartbreaking."

Tracy Wright is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital. Send story tips to Tracy.Wright@fox.com.

title: Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq investigated over on-set rape and assault allegations
excerpt:
Actor and author are alleged to have attacked and gang-raped a woman while filming together in 2018

French police are investigating allegations that the actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel H...
body_text:
Actor and author are alleged to have attacked and gang-raped a woman while filming together in 2018

French police are investigating allegations that the actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot.

The alleged attack took place in December 2018 during the shooting of Thalasso, a film starring the two men as versions of themselves who meet at a health spa and have long philosophical conversations while in white bath-robes.

Two sources following the case confirmed to Agence France-Presse on Friday that a police investigation was under way.

The investigative website Mediapart reported this week that an actor, given the pseudonym Alexandra, had made a complaint to police in 2025.

Alexandra, an eastern European actor and dancer who was 32 at the time and working in France, told Mediapart that she was attacked by Depardieu and Houellebecq as they pinned her down during one scene and while cameras filmed.

Mediapart reported that Alexandra described being “in a state of stupefaction and disconnect”. In her police complaint she had spoken of “deep humiliation” and “indescribable shame”.

The film’s director, Guillaume Nicloux, had been accused of complicity in the sexual abuse, AFP reported.

Nicloux told Mediapart that at the moment of filming he had not “noticed any constraint”, but he had “apologised” to Alexandra.

Alexandra’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. Depardieu’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment. The Guardian contacted Houellebecq’s publishers, who did not respond.

This week Depardieu, 77, dropped his appeal against a 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a different film set in 2021, and apologised to them.

At his trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021. His suspended sentence will now stand and his name has been added to France’s sex offender register.

After Depardieu’s apology this week, the assistant director whom he sexually assaulted said: “The monster of cinema has fallen.”

Depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France. He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously.

He has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year.

In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and said any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote.

Houellebecq, 70, who is among France’s most translated authors, is also under investigation for alleged incitement to discrimination in France over comments he made in 2022 about Muslims.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Police search for teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction
excerpt:
Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s

Police are searching for a missing chemistry teacher convicted of sexual relationships ...
body_text:
Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s

Police are searching for a missing chemistry teacher convicted of sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s after she did not turn up to her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, was not found at her Hemel Hempstead home by Metropolitan police officers after her failure to attend Harrow crown court in north London on Friday, where a warrant was issued for her arrest.

Bowen’s barrister, Mark Kimsey, told the court she was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been “concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages” from her.

The former teacher, who was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy when they were aged about 14 to 15, was convicted in August of seven counts of indecent assault and granted bail before her sentencing.

Judge Karim Ezzat issued a warrant for her arrest, which he said was “not backed by bail”.

Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said Bowen’s partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the home address when officers arrived, but Bowen was not.

Gomersall earlier told the court there was “no evidence” that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and that information from her partner was “suggestive of refusal rather than inability” to attend.

The Met said: “On Friday 20 November, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow crown court for sentencing. A warrant has been issued for her arrest, and inquiries to locate her are ongoing.”

The trial heard that Bowen was in her mid-20s when she taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London.

Jurors heard she had worn short, tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to “a Sabrina Carpenter video”.

One victim told jurors he had had sex with her “about 20 or 30 times” over several months, considered her his girlfriend and kept it secret. He said it had led to “the destruction of my education”.

The second victim described spending lunchtimes with Bowen in a cafe, where he was “goaded” into kissing her by other boys and recalled touching her breasts.

Bowen denied the allegations as “total fabrication” and claimed a medical condition made sex difficult and painful. She denied flirting, saying: “I didn’t flirt with students, I was just friendly.” Defending her clothes, she said she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher”.

title: White supremacist convicted of planning bomb attack on asylum seekers in Hull
excerpt:
Mikka Anderson stockpiled weapons and tried to recruit accomplice for attack on Royal Hotel

A white supremacist has been found guilty of planning a firebomb terror attack on asylum seekers in Hull.

...
body_text:
Mikka Anderson stockpiled weapons and tried to recruit accomplice for attack on Royal Hotel

A white supremacist has been found guilty of planning a firebomb terror attack on asylum seekers in Hull.

Mikka Anderson, 24, stockpiled weapons including napalm, knives and a crossbow for an assault designed to kill as many people as possible, Newcastle crown court heard.

The British man, from Hull, tried to recruit an accomplice for an attack on the city’s Royal Hotel, which housed asylum seekers until September this year. However, his plan unravelled when that man went to the police.

Anderson had denied preparing an act of terrorism but was found guilty on Friday. The judge, Mrs Justice Lambert, told the defendant he should expect a “very significant” prison term when he is sentenced next year.

Anderson first made contact with his intended accomplice through social media, knowing that the man – who cannot be identified by the media – had been involved in anti-migrant disorder in the city.

On a secure messaging platform, Anderson told the man he was in a group of “white Christian nationalists” whose “main objective is fighting back against Islam, paedophile elites and Jews”.

The two men met in the city centre when Anderson outlined his plan to attack Hull’s Royal Hotel “and to kill as many of the migrants who were housed inside it as possible”, said Adam Birkby, prosecuting.

During the trial, the intended accomplice told jurors Anderson explained his rationale for targeting the hotel, saying: “He said it was full of nonces, rapists, people that shouldn’t be in our country.”

After the informer told police about the plot, Anderson was arrested. Knives, a crossbow and petrol bombs were found during a search of his home.

He had made or attempted to create napalm, gunpowder and fuses, the court heard, and carried out reconnaissance on the hotel, which housed migrants until September this year.

The trial heard that Anderson, who grew up in France and Spain before moving to the North York Moors, had previously tried to join the Royal Marines.

Anderson had also tried to buy a piece of land in Devon with fellow rightwingers, who planned to use it as a shooting ground and a site to practise tactics.

Earlier, the trial heard, he had looked into Islam but turned away from it and had also previously been a Mormon.

He then developed an interest in the extreme-right following the Southport riots, finding a sense of “brotherhood” with others after experiencing an isolated childhood, jurors were told.

title: Latest botched execution prompts calls for US moratorium on lethal injections
excerpt:
Reinaldo Dennes screamed in pain and took over an hour to die – but Texas officials branded the execution a success

A botched execution in Texas on Thursday night that lasted more than an hour and ca...
body_text:
Reinaldo Dennes screamed in pain and took over an hour to die – but Texas officials branded the execution a success

A botched execution in Texas on Thursday night that lasted more than an hour and caused the prisoner to scream out, begging the Lord to end his suffering, has led to renewed calls for a nationwide moratorium that would pause all lethal injections.

It took 63 minutes for Reinaldo Dennes, 70, to be proclaimed dead in the Huntsville penitentiary. The execution team had struggled to find a vein through which a lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital could be administered.

Descriptions of the botched lethal injection bear chilling similarities to the recent failed execution in Tennessee of Christa Pike who in September became the only person ever to survive a full dose of execution drugs. Both Dennes and Pike were subjected to lethal injection protocols using pentobarbital, in both cases staff struggled to establish intravenous lines, and in both the prisoner expressed experiencing excruciating pain and burning sensations.

“The world saw what happened to Christa Pike, and now to Mr Dennes,” said Robin Maher, executive director of the authoritative Death Penalty Information Center. “The question now is, how many more of these botched executions will be tolerated by the American people?”

A harrowing eyewitness account of the night’s events was given by the prisoner’s spiritual adviser, the Rev Jeff Hood, who stood beside the gurney with his hand on Dennes’s shoulder. Hood describes how for up to five minutes Dennes fought against the pain.

“The pain!” Dennes shouted, according to Hood’s account.

“My leg, my leg, my leg,” he screamed, adding that his leg was “on fire”.

Hood writes in his account that Dennes “shifted on the gurney, back and forth, back and forth. He contorted. He grabbed hold of the leather straps and pulled against them until his body lifted. His shoulder drove up into my palm. Then it fell away. Then it drove up again. Twice he screamed, ‘It’s not working like it’s supposed to. Fuck. Fuck. Fuck. What is going on? Fuck. Fuck. Fuck.’”

Throughout the ordeal, Hood reports, the prisoner continued to pray, begging for an end to it.

“Take me home, Father. I don’t think this is normal. Take me, Father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.”

Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the 1996 death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was shot and killed in Houston.

Maya Foa, chief executive of the human rights group Reprieve, called for a moratorium on lethal injections. She said: “Lethal injection is torture – and Reinaldo Dennes was not sentenced to be tortured. Even the most ardent supporters of capital punishment must recognise that the dominant method of execution in the US is broken and cannot be allowed to continue.”

The Texas department of criminal justice insisted that the execution went fully according to plan. Its spokeswoman, Amanda Hernandez, told the New York Times that “as far as this agency is concerned, it is 100 percent not a botched execution. This was a successful execution, and we did follow all of the proper protocols to do it correctly.”

But such a blanket dismissal of any concerns failed to dampen a chorus of criticism. “Americans are now seeing the harsh reality of the death penalty, and I just don’t know how much longer state officials think they can double down on a story that is false,” Maher said.

Texas has been under the spotlight for many years for the way it obtains and stores its stocks of lethal execution drugs, a manoeuvre which it is careful to shroud in secrecy in an attempt to avoid public scrutiny. In the wake of an international boycott, the state’s prison service has taken to buying pentobarbital from compounding pharmacies that make up the chemicals to order.

Lawyers for condemned prisoners have long argued that the supplies can be of variable quality and are often held by the state beyond their expiration dates, running the risk of causing excruciating deaths.

The way that Texas conducts executions is likely to come under fresh review given the political upheaval that the state has experienced in the midterm elections. Not only did the governor’s mansion fall to the Democrat Gina Hinojosa, but Democrats flipped 20 state House seats as well as taking all seats up for election in the Texas supreme court and court of criminal appeals that have enormous power over capital cases.

Jonathan Groner, an expert on execution methods and emeritus professor of clinical surgery at Ohio State University, said that the Dennes execution illustrated why lethal injections were a “medical charade”. He said: “They imitate general anesthesia which is done in hospitals across the country thousands of times a day, by people with expertise, but when it is done in the death chamber without necessary equipment or skills, people suffer.”

Groner said that the location of the two IV lines placed in Dennes’s body – in a foot and in his shoulder – indicated that the execution team was struggling. “Placing IVs in the neck is very painful and difficult, and a last resort; and the foot is not a top choice because there is a long way to the heart for the medication to be circulated.”

He added: “It’s time for the medical profession to make a stand on executions. People are being tortured. We need to stop, and take a hard look at why we are still doing this.”

title: Fired White House press secretary Katie Zacharia under California state bar investigation
excerpt:
Zacharia’s spokesperson called allegations she falsely represented herself as an attorney ‘baseless’

Katie Zacharia, the former White House press secretary hired and fired in the same week, is under ...
body_text:
Zacharia’s spokesperson called allegations she falsely represented herself as an attorney ‘baseless’

Katie Zacharia, the former White House press secretary hired and fired in the same week, is under investigation by the state bar of California for claiming to be a lawyer despite never passing the bar exam.

Earlier this month, the state bar of California informed Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog group, that it had assigned an investigator and legal adviser to investigate Zacharia after the organization filed a complaint.

Before her short stint as Donald Trump’s press secretary, Zacharia repeatedly represented herself as a lawyer on cable news programs and had claimed on her LinkedIn profile that she served as the general counsel for a non-profit organization in California.

Trump also identified Zacharia as an “attorney” when announcing her appointment.

While Zacharia received a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011, she never passed the bar exam in California or any other US state.

“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the director of the Campaign for Accountability, said in a statement.

“We’re pleased the California Bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating,” Kuppersmith added.

A spokesperson for Zacharia said in a statement to the Guardian: “These are baseless allegations. This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar’s time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing.”

Zacharia previously defended describing herself as a “lawyer”, claiming there was a difference between a “lawyer” and an “attorney”, a title reserved for those licensed to practice law. In her email to the Guardian, Zacharia linked to an American Bar Association Journal article distinguishing the two terms.

The Guardian has asked the state bar of California for comment.

The Campaign for Accountability had submitted a complaint to the state bar of California in mid-October.

“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has,” the non-profit watchdog organization wrote in their complaint.

Zacharia became the shortest-serving White House press secretary when she replaced Karoline Leavitt in mid-October for just five days. From the start, she struggled to fit into the role, stumbling over words during her first press briefing and only taking questions from predominantly conservative media outlets.

title: Cost of living protests sweep across Europe
excerpt:
Protests took place across European cities on Friday as marches were held over the cost of living and other issues, including housing shortages and underfunding in education.

Demonstrations took plac...
body_text:
Protests took place across European cities on Friday as marches were held over the cost of living and other issues, including housing shortages and underfunding in education.

Demonstrations took place in Germany, France, Croatia, Italy, the United Kingdom and elsewhere, attracting a lot of young adults.

The BBC's Europe correspondent, Nick Beake, has been reporting from Rome, where thousands of people took part in a march organised by Italy's main trade union.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Resurfaced video appears to show NYC mayor arrested by NYPD group he is disbanding
excerpt: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani tweeted video of himself getting arrested at a protest against landlords and evictions in 2021 by an officer who appears to be part of the NYPD's Strategic Response ...
body_text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani tweeted video of himself getting arrested at a protest against landlords and evictions in 2021 by an officer who appears to be part of the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, which he is now disbanding.

Years before New York City's socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani ordered the dismantling of a specialized police task force, he'd been detained by its members, resurfaced video the mayor himself tweeted in 2021 appears to show.

The video appears to show the arresting officer's vest reading "NYPD Special Response Group" across the back during a protest against an end to the city's COVID-era moratorium on evictions.

The mayor's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

MICHAEL RUIZ: NEW YORK'S GUTTED POLICE UNIT WAS MORE THAN A PROTEST SQUAD

In this still image taken from video, an NYPD member whose uniform reads "Special Response Group" across the back can be seen escorting Zohran Mamdani away from a protest with his wrists bound behind his back. Now the New York City mayor, Mamdani has announced the SRG will be disbanded. (Zohran Mamdani/X)

Mamdani announced that the group will be dissolved at a news briefing early Monday. He had campaigned on the issue in part due to the unit's role in responding to organized protests — and riots — including those that exploded after George Floyd's death in 2020, demonstrations against Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Israel's war with Palestinian Hamas terrorists.

The images were recirculated earlier this week by Crain's New York, a local outlet focused on business, politics and real estate.

A second video, recorded by the local ABC affiliate, appears to show Mamdani arrested again by the unit shortly before he announced his mayoral bid in 2024.

On Monday, Mamdani said he would disband the group and divvy up its responsibilities — which included crowd control at protests and riots, critical incident response and counterterrorism — between three new entities and the NYPD's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau.

One of the new units is the unarmed Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD). This civilian team won't have arrest authority.

The back of the officer's uniform can be seen in the video. (Zohran Mamdani/X)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"His voters won’t care," said Joseph Giacalone, a retired NYPD sergeant and criminal justice professor. "These transplants are all renters using mommy and daddy’s money to live in NYC, and when things go south, and they will, they’ll flee back home."

NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI SAYS HE WON'T FIRE NYPD COMMISSIONER JESSICA TISCH DESPITE SOCIALIST PRESSURE

The NYPD Strategic Response Group (SRG) monitors a crowd outside 26 Federal Plaza on Oct. 21, 2025 in New York City. (Photo by Adam Gray/Getty Images)

Upcoming events like the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and New Year's ball drop will not be impacted since the changes aren't slated to go into effect until spring 2027.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement that the restructuring would not "diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat."
