title: EDF snaps up 1.3m more customers after Utilita takeover
excerpt:
Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier brings account base up to 6m after purchase of pay-as-you-go supplier

EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m custo...
body_text:
Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier brings account base up to 6m after purchase of pay-as-you-go supplier

EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita.

Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed.

The pair will continue to serve their customers independently until the deal concludes. Utilita customers will be contacted about any changes to their service.

After the deal, EDF has promised to continue to operate from Utilita’s headquarters near Southampton which is the base for about 600of Utilita’s employees.

EDF, which is owned by the French state, set out the takeover plans a year after it completed a deal to take on 47,000 standard credit accounts from Utilita which said it hoped to sharpen its focus on smart pay-as-you-go customers.

The deal is likely to have helped bolster Utilita’s financial position, which briefly fell short of the industry regulator Ofgem’s tougher new financial resilience tests in an industry assessment in September 2025.

Utilita confirmed that it was one of five suppliers which had failed to meet Ofgem’s financial rules last year, but said it was able to comply with the standards within months of the regulator’s red flag.

For EDF, the deal will help to bolster its business as most large suppliers continue to lose customers to smaller rivals. EDF lost about 280,000 customer accounts in the year after July 2025, while British Gas, Scottish Power and E.ON were also losing customers. Octopus Energy, the country’s largest supplier, is the only big energy company which has continued to grow its market share.

Utilita was founded in 2003 as a specialist prepay energy supplier, and became the first supplier to install a smart meter in 2008.

Its pioneering approach to smart metering helped the company to modernise pay-as-you-go energy by allowing customers to top-up via an app, website, or by phone rather than visit a corner shop or post office to pay for credit on a plastic card or key.

Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF’s UK business, said Utilita would bring “further expertise” to the supplier, marking “a significant step” in EDF’s ambition to grow its UK customer business.

“Together, we will have the scale and skills to keep developing services and support for the households who rely on us,” Rossi said.

Bill Bullen, the founder of Utilita, said the deal would ensure that Utilita could continue to provide “best-in-class smart prepay solutions to Britain’s households”.

The deal comes as households prepare for a sharp rise in energy bills this winter. On Wednesday, the consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast the quarterly industry price cap would jump 26% from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.

title: Why is Pete Hegseth strengthening US military ties with Venezuela?
excerpt:
Hegseth unveils new US-Venezuela military deal

United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a new cooperation agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooper...
body_text:
Hegseth unveils new US-Venezuela military deal

United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a new cooperation agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooperation between the two countries.

The Pentagon chief’s announcement came during an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday. The US says the agreement will help fight drug trafficking and improve security in the region. Venezuela says it will help strengthen its military without compromising its sovereignty.

But why is an agreement happening now, and what does each side stand to gain?

The US and Venezuela have agreed to strengthen military cooperation in several areas, including joint training, intelligence sharing, military equipment and border security.

Hegseth met Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez and Defence Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez in Caracas. He said the agreement would allow the two countries’ armed forces to work together to combat drug trafficking and armed groups operating in Venezuela.

Rodriguez described Hegseth’s visit as an extraordinary step in relations between the two countries.

She said renewed military cooperation would help improve troop training, modernise equipment and give armed forces access to new technologies.

Her government said the country’s armed forces, known as the Bolivarian National Armed Forces (FANB), would benefit directly from the agreement.

However, the full terms of the agreement have not been made public, including details of how the two countries would carry out joint military operations.

The Trump administration said closer military cooperation with Venezuela will help fight drug trafficking and armed groups, and improve security in the region.

Hegseth said the agreement should help Venezuela regain control of areas where armed groups and drug trafficking networks operate.

But political analyst Carlos Pina said the timing of the visit is important, particularly after the Democrats won the midterm elections in the US.

“I think many of the things happening between the United States and Venezuela are closely related to the November 3 election results,” Pina said.

He explained that the Democrats have already said they aim to increase scrutiny of US foreign policy towards Venezuela, including the agreements reached with Caracas during 2026, after US forces abducted then-President Nicolas Maduro and took him to New York. The US has since, in effect, taken control of Venezuela’s oil industry — the country has the world’s largest oil reserves.

Pina also pointed out the recent attempt to impeach Hegseth. “I think this Hegseth visit also falls within that framework, to get ahead of what will be the debate in the new US Congress.”

On November 10, the House of Representatives voted 211-204 against impeaching Hegseth for now, but Democrats could try again after January, with their new majority in the House.

The November resolution against Hegseth, introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, included eight articles of impeachment related to the US-Israel war on Iran, military strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats and the January operation that ousted Maduro from power.

Massie said Hegseth ordered an act of war against Venezuela without congressional authorisation. He argued that the operation went beyond arresting Maduro on drug trafficking charges and was also intended to give Washington control over Venezuela’s oil reserves.

“Secretary Hegseth executed unlawful orders effecting the removal of the President of a sovereign nation, placed boots on the ground, conducted preparatory bombardments, inflicted substantial casualties, and subsequently caused regime change, each of which constitutes acts of war,” Massie said in the impeachment resolution.

Pina believes Hegseth’s visit is partly aimed at defending Trump’s policy in Venezuela before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

“Hegseth goes to Venezuela, which is probably one of Trump’s few foreign policy successes, to show the American public that the plan they are carrying out in Venezuela benefits US national interests,” he said.

Rodriguez and her government welcomed the agreement, saying it will help strengthen the country’s forces and improve its training and access to technology.

Venezuelan officials have also stressed that the cooperation must respect the country’s sovereignty and constitution.

But analysts say the agreement may also signal Rodriguez’s efforts to remain in power following Maduro’s ousting.

“The simple answer is that they want to remain in power as long as possible,” Phil Gunson, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.

He said Rodriguez’s government faces considerable pressure from Washington. “If they decline to cooperate, they have been told they will suffer the same fate as Maduro, or worse.”

He also pointed to Washington’s financial leverage over Caracas.

“The US currently controls most of Venezuela’s foreign earnings, in the form of revenue from oil sales, and can cut off the funds whenever it wishes,” Gunson said.

Since Maduro’s ousting in January, revenue from Venezuelan oil sales has been deposited into US-controlled accounts, with Washington supervising the release of funds to Caracas.

According to a Department of State report released on November 12, more than $12bn from Venezuela’s oil and other natural resources passed through these accounts between January and September.

The US government said nearly 99 percent of the money had been disbursed mostly to individuals and businesses in Venezuela through commercial banks. But the agreement means Caracas depends on Washington to approve the release of money from these accounts, potentially giving the Trump administration tools to put pressure on Rodriguez’s government.

Pina described the Venezuelan government’s approach as “a calculation of survival”.

“They are capable of yielding in certain areas to the US government, as long as their hold on government is not affected or threatened,” he told Al Jazeera.

Pina also said Rodriguez was trying to buy time, particularly as Democrats prepare to take control of the US Congress in January.

“She gains time,” he said, suggesting that greater congressional scrutiny of Trump’s Venezuela policies could eventually give Caracas more room to negotiate.

One of the key questions, say analysts, is whether closer cooperation with Washington could lead to changes within Venezuela’s armed forces, many of whose senior officers served under Maduro.

Gunson said much would depend on Washington’s intentions.

“Will Washington seek to reform the security forces, whose leaders it has accused of drug trafficking, human rights abuses and collaboration with Colombian guerrillas and other armed groups?” he said.

He also explained Venezuela’s military is not in a position to resist US influence.

“In its current state, the military as an institution is not in a position to resist US influence, for good or ill,” he said.

But he explained that some senior officers could try to sabotage the process if they feared prosecution or losing their positions.

Separately, Venezuelan Defence Minister Gonzalez Lopez also issued his first statement since taking office.

He said the new relationship follows the “painful events of January 3”, when US forces removed Maduro from power.

Gonzalez Lopez said military cooperation with Washington would follow Venezuela’s constitution and respect the country’s “sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity”.

He also stressed that Venezuela’s armed forces would retain control over their own leadership, command and operations.

There is no clarity on the terms of the agreement.

But Pina said the agreement seems to focus on limited military cooperation, particularly operations against armed groups and drug trafficking networks along the Venezuela-Colombia border.

Pina said the two countries could carry out joint military operations, including air raids against armed groups operating in the area.

But he believes Venezuela’s military will be reluctant to give the US a much larger role.

“The Venezuelan armed forces are not going to concede beyond that,” he said.

Pina argued that Washington needs a stronger military presence in Venezuela if it wants to maintain its influence over the country’s political transition, particularly because armed forces remain under the governing party’s control.

The agreement could affect other countries, particularly neighbouring Colombia, which shares a long border with Venezuela.

Several Colombian armed groups operate on both sides of the border, including the National Liberation Army (ELN), which has been fighting the Colombian government for decades.

Pina said the joint military operations could weaken these groups and reduce their ability to operate across the border.

However, on Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella had rejected a US proposal to allow joint military operations on its territory.

But De La Espriella denied the NYT report, saying Colombia wanted to strengthen military cooperation with Washington, although the presence of foreign troops would require congressional approval.

Hegseth also rejected the report, calling it “totally false”.

Gunson said Trump sees Venezuela as a major success and as a model for US relations with Latin America. But he said the results of the midterm elections could change how governments in the region respond to Washington.

“Governments in the region that seemed bound to fall into line with the US hemispheric security policy may start to think again,” Gunson said.

Pina also believes the agreement with Venezuela could raise concerns in other Latin American countries, including Mexico, about the possibility of US military operations on their territory.

“I think what happened with Nicolas Maduro marked a before and after in Donald Trump’s regional security policy,” Pina said.

He argued that the January operation showed Washington was prepared to use military force to pursue its interests, even when such actions could violate international law.

But Pina questioned whether the agreement represents a long-term change in US policy towards the region, or is primarily a political response to the recent attempt to impeach Hegseth.

title: Gaza Syndrome: Why Israeli soldiers’ trauma erases Palestinian victims
excerpt:
Cost of War: The trauma Israeli soldiers bring home from Gaza | Al Jazeera Originals

Editor’s note: This article contains references to suicide and graphic descriptions of combat.

If you or someone ...
body_text:
Cost of War: The trauma Israeli soldiers bring home from Gaza | Al Jazeera Originals

Editor’s note: This article contains references to suicide and graphic descriptions of combat.

If you or someone you know is at risk of suicide, support is available through international crisis helplines.

“I think our army is the most moral army in the world.”

Itay Sagi, a reservist in the Maglan unit, describes killing Hamas fighters inside Israel after October 7, 2023.

“I didn’t choose to kill people. I had to,” he says.

His grief is for his friends. Sagi wants to go back and fight. He does not mention the Palestinians killed in Gaza.

Boris Shtonda, who served with an Israeli special forces unit, lost a leg when an explosive device detonated inside a building in Gaza in November 2023, killing four of his friends.

“We lost our friends, we lost our families, we lost everything,” he says.

The Israeli soldiers in the film “Gaza Syndrome” speak of nightmares, panic, addiction and Israelis who died by suicide. They speak, too, of wanting to return to fight. In hours of testimony, the Palestinians of Gaza are almost entirely absent.

The overwhelming weight of Israel’s war has fallen on Palestinians in Gaza: their children, homes and hospitals. Israeli forces have killed at least 74,700 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, according to Al Jazeera reporting. In September 2025, an independent UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed genocide in Gaza. The soldiers in this film are part of those forces.

Guy Zaken, a military bulldozer driver, told an Israeli parliamentary committee that soldiers had to “run over “‘terrorists’, dead and alive, in the hundreds”. His co-driver, Eliran Mizrahi, spent 186 days in Gaza demolishing homes and died by suicide two days before he was due to return. “He got out of Gaza, but Gaza did not get out of him,” his mother told CNN.

The question is not whether the Israeli soldiers’ psychological injuries are real. It is what psychological injury means when it is joined to denial, impunity and the absence of remorse.

In The Wretched of the Earth, the mid-20th century psychiatrist and political philosopher Frantz Fanon observed that colonial violence inflicts severe psychiatric trauma on both the colonised and the perpetrators. When soldiers carry out systematic destruction and violence, the psychological toll cannot be separated from the political structure that enables and ignores it.

An Al Jazeera Investigative Unit examination of more than 2,500 Israeli soldiers’ social media accounts documented wanton destruction, abuse of detainees, and the use of Palestinian civilians as human shields.

The scale of the psychological crisis is growing. Nearly 30,000 Israeli soldiers and security personnel wounded since October 7 have entered the Defence Ministry’s rehabilitation system, the ministry said in October.

About 63 percent have psychological injuries, with thousands formally diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and acute stress reactions following prolonged combat exposure. The Israeli army says 22 soldiers died by suicide in 2025, one more than in 2024, up from 17 in 2023. An Israeli parliament Research and Information Center report recorded 279 suicide attempts between January 2024 and July 2025. Combat soldiers accounted for 78 percent of the deaths by suicide in 2024.

Mohanad Mustafa, a scholar of Israeli society, told Al Jazeera Israel faces “a psychological crisis among thousands of soldiers, but no moral crisis”.

He says many soldiers feel no remorse for violations of international law. “This indicates a very significant moral decline in Israeli society.”

Israel’s public culture has helped make that denial possible. Oren Ziv, an Israeli journalist with +972 Magazine, says soldiers he interviewed described “an atmosphere of revenge, that everything is allowed”. They could shoot if they saw movement, he says, or if they were bored, and “nobody will investigate it”.

Daniel Bar-Tal, a political psychologist, says soldiers in Gaza still confront Palestinian suffering “to some extent”, even when they deny it or refuse to see it.

This suppressed awareness, he said, creates a quiet, internal fracture, a psychological burden that deepens precisely because the trauma cannot be fully acknowledged or resolved without confronting the suffering of those they harmed.

Ashira Darwish, a Palestinian trauma therapist and survivor of severe trauma and torture who created Active Meditation to heal from full-body paralysis, believes Israeli soldiers can enter Gaza, shoot children and burn homes only by suppressing their own humanity. She and other trauma experts emphasise that returning reservists undergo a severe psychological transition when re-entering civilian life after engaging in continuous combat.

“Someone who can exterminate an entire people while sitting there laughing will carry a psychological impact.”

Darwish describes reservists returning from Gaza to a hospital, office or school within a week or two. She warns of anger, substance addiction, domestic conflict, and sudden outbursts of violence as untreated combat trauma manifests in everyday interactions. “Where are they supposed to go with everything they have done?”

Israel’s Observatory on Femicide recorded 34 femicides in 2025, a 48 percent rise from 23 in 2024. Firearms were the most common weapon for the first time. Women’s groups warned early in the war that combat trauma and expanded access to guns could heighten the risk of domestic violence. There is no official data proving that returning soldiers caused the rise, and the Observatory found no link between licenced guns and femicide. The warning is about a society saturated with weapons, fear and impunity, not a claim that every soldier becomes violent at home.

In Qusra, a Palestinian village south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, the film finds the other end of that impunity. Abdul Azim al-Wadi, a former head of the village council, says Israeli settlers killed his brother Ibrahim and nephew Ahmad, shot two of his sons and burned his son’s and daughter’s homes.

“The occupation army is the continuation of the settlers’ attacks,” he says. “They play the role together.”

Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.

The same impunity is visible in Gaza. In NAZA, a documentary built on anonymous testimony from Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, sources describe civilian deaths factored into military decisions and targets watched inside their homes. The Israeli army called NAZA a “manipulative depiction of reality”.

In March, Israel dropped charges against five soldiers accused of sexually abusing a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention facility.

A few do not accept the orders to serve in the army. Itamar Greenberg chose military prison over conscription. Iddo Elam said: “I do not want to hold a weapon towards innocent people.”

Their refusal matters because it shows the violence is not inevitable, and neither is the story Israel tells about it.

Bar-Tal offers his country a choice: “Cut the violence or cut the narrative.”

title: 'You will regret it': Angry resident confronts Democratic mayor during chaotic council meeting
excerpt: A Sacramento City Council meeting descended into chaos after a resident confronted Mayor Kevin McCarty, threatened his political career and attempted to publicly reveal his home address, prompting off...
body_text:
A Sacramento City Council meeting descended into chaos after a resident confronted Mayor Kevin McCarty, threatened his political career and attempted to publicly reveal his home address, prompting officials to cut her microphone and recess the meeting. (City of Sacramento via YouTube)

A Sacramento City Council meeting descended into chaos Tuesday after an angry resident threatened the Democratic mayor's political career and attempted to publicly reveal his home address, prompting officials to cut her microphone and temporarily recess the meeting.

Video from Tuesday's city council livestream reviewed by Fox News Digital showed a woman confronting Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty during the public comment portion of the meeting, warning that protesters would continue disrupting city business if officials failed to address their concerns.

"If you do not vote in our interest again, you will regret it," the woman said. "We protest. We stop things. We shut things down, Kevin. And careers."

The woman then suggested that McCarty's political career had run its course.

MEMPHIS CITY COUNCIL DEVOLVES INTO CHAOS AFTER DATA CENTER MORATORIUM VOTE POSTPONED

A woman warned Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty that he would "regret it" if city officials continued voting against protesters' interests during a heated City Council meeting. (Sacramento City Council livestream)

"It's time for your f---ing career to end," she said, before raising the possibility of his retirement.

As council officials repeatedly attempted to restore order, someone in the audience also urged the angry woman to show decorum.

The confrontation escalated further when the woman threatened to disclose the mayor's home address.

"I do not give a f--- about your privacy," she shouted. "Do you want everyone to know your address? Because now I know your address."

Her microphone appeared to be cut as she began reciting what she claimed was the mayor's address, and a council official warned her against disclosing private information.

'I BASICALLY SNAPPED': NEW JERSEY MAYOR CHARGES AT RESIDENT DURING CHAOTIC COUNCIL MEETING

A Sacramento City Council meeting descended into chaos on Nov. 17 after a resident confronted Mayor Kevin McCarty and attempted to publicly disclose what she claimed was his home address. (Sacramento City Council livestream)

As shouting erupted in the council chambers, officials called a recess and council members left the dais.

Approximately 20 minutes later, council members returned and resumed public comment. No audience members were removed, The Sacramento Bee reported.

According to the newspaper, the confrontation with the woman, identified by the outlet as a local immigration activist, unfolded amid ongoing tensions over the city's immigration enforcement policies and its cooperation with federal authorities.

Earlier in the meeting, McCarty announced that the council would postpone consideration of a $3.7 million Department of Homeland Security grant agreement amid questions about potential data-sharing provisions.

Tuesday's incident marked the fifth time this year that Sacramento City Council members had recessed a meeting because of audience disruptions, according to The Sacramento Bee. The repeated confrontations have largely stemmed from activists' concerns about immigration enforcement and the city's sanctuary policies, the outlet reported.

DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED'

Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty faced a heated confrontation during a City Council meeting Tuesday after a resident threatened his political career and attempted to reveal his home address. (Sacramento City Council livestream)

The mayor's office declined to comment on the incident to Fox News Digital.

This week's outburst comes months after Fox News Digital reported that a live microphone captured McCarty and Vice Mayor Karina Talamantes discussing whether disruptive protesters could be barred from future council meetings.

"We should go over this disruptions thing, because if we want to ban somebody in the future, like to take them out, we have to point out specifically," Talamantes was heard saying during the July meeting.

"I know, but the city attorney said we can't do that," McCarty responded.

The woman who confronted McCarty on Tuesday also appeared during the July meeting, when she shouted at the mayor, "Kevin, listen to me. Stop being an a--hole, dude. Listen to your f---ing constituents."

Following the July incident, McCarty told Fox News Digital that council leaders were responsible for ensuring public meetings remained accessible and orderly.

Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty faced a heated confrontation during a City Council meeting Tuesday after a resident threatened his political career and attempted to reveal his home address. (Sacramento City Council livestream)

The mayor's office declined to comment on the incident to Fox News Digital.

This week's outburst comes months after Fox News Digital reported that a live microphone captured McCarty and Vice Mayor Karina Talamantes discussing whether disruptive protesters could be barred from future council meetings.

"We should go over this disruptions thing, because if we want to ban somebody in the future, like to take them out, we have to point out specifically," Talamantes was heard saying during the July meeting.

"I know, but the city attorney said we can't do that," McCarty responded.

The woman who confronted McCarty on Tuesday also appeared during the July meeting, when she shouted at the mayor, "Kevin, listen to me. Stop being an a--hole, dude. Listen to your f---ing constituents."

Following the July incident, McCarty told Fox News Digital that council leaders were responsible for ensuring public meetings remained accessible and orderly.

Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Watchdog flags fraud, failed Pentagon audit as defense priorities
excerpt: Days after the Pentagon failed its ninth consecutive audit, its oversight office ranked eliminating fraud and achieving a clean financial audit among the Defense Department’s most pressing strategic c...
body_text:
Days after the Pentagon failed its ninth consecutive audit, its oversight office ranked eliminating fraud and achieving a clean financial audit among the Defense Department’s most pressing strategic challenges for the upcoming fiscal year.

As the Trump administration asks Congress for a record $1.5 trillion for national defense, the Department of Defense Inspector General this week released an annual report listing the seven top hurdles facing the department as it executes the National Defense Strategy. The priorities — not ranked in order of priority, according to the office — range from deterring China to energizing the defense-industrial base to supporting warfighters and financial transparency.

The 2026 National Defense Strategy elevated defense of the “U.S. Homeland” and the Western Hemisphere above countering China and declared the “Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine,” prioritizing American dominance in the hemisphere and American access to the Panama Canal and Gulf of Mexico.

Here are the challenges identified by the IG’s office.

“Considering the Department’s extensive operations and sizeable budget, the risk of fraud is inherent,” the report said, emphasizing that the Pentagon has the largest discretionary federal budget and is asking Congress for a 42% increase in its current funding.

Hegseth has campaigned against government waste and pledged to eliminate redundancy in the Pentagon. In 2025, amid an investigation into his own Signal use, Hegseth issued a memo addressing reforms to the IG office. He told military leaders that the office’s systems had been “weaponized, putting complainers, ideologues and poor performers in the driver’s seat.”

In 2018, after the Pentagon failed its first-ever audit, Congress gave the Defense Department 10 years — until Dec. 31, 2028 — to pass. Though it failed again this year, an official told Reuters that the audit found 14 of 25 Pentagon entities’ passing financial statements, up from 11 the prior year.

Auditors are now using artificial intelligence to process and test more data on many of the Pentagon’s outdated systems. The department established Joint Task Force-Audit, which is a group of civilians, service members and private sector experts to address continued issues.

The National Defense Strategy places defense of the “U.S. homeland” and Western Hemisphere in the top slot. The IG identified strain on forces deployed to the U.S. border and said it is currently investigating the effectiveness of domestic National Guard deployments. The report also flagged gaps in infrastructure cybersecurity and in counter-unmanned aerial capabilities around important installations.

Bumped to second priority, the U.S. is focusing on deterrence in the Indo-Pacific by building a strong posture in the First Island Chain, a set of Pacific archipelagos.

The IG identified issues “with the readiness of forward-stationed logistics networks, condition and availability of prepositioned equipment, resilience of contested maritime sustainment routes, and the Department’s ability to disperse and operate airpower from multiple locations in the U.S. Pacific Command area of responsibility.”

The services have begun to prepare for a Pacific-oriented fight. For instance, the Army is accelerating development of its next-generation assault tiltrotor aircraft, the Cheyenne II, designed for use in a Pacific theater.

Burden sharing has become a signature phrase for the Trump administration, from discussions about rotational forces in Europe to counterterrorism operations in Africa to deterrence in the Indo-Pacific.

The office “identified lessons learned from 10 years of reports related to burden sharing with international partners, noting lack of proper reimbursement by international partners for supplies and services provided by the Department,” the report said. It did not provide specific examples or list the international partners in question.

The report said the IG continues to find production shortfalls and, in some cases, a lack of accountability for major defense contractors that fall short of requirements.

The Defense Department “is sometimes so dependent on certain contractors that it continues to give them funds even when they fail to deliver or delay delivery by years,” the report said.

Additionally, the agency said contractors had not delivered the agreed-upon amount of munitions on time, leading to diminished stockpiles of critical munitions.

Earlier this year, the agency also found that the Pentagon’s drive to get weapons faster bypassed acquisition steps meant to ensure new systems work before reaching the force.

The new report flagged issues with overseas medical care — including patient safety — the health of trainees, housing quality and issues in the review process for child abuse accusations at childcare centers.

According to a new Pentagon directive, all military services must now resolve emergency living conditions within 24 hours or relocate the service member.

Eve Sampson is a reporter and former Army officer. She has covered conflict across the world, writing for The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Associated Press.

title: Japan scrambles fighter jets after Russian aircraft breach airspace amid rising Pacific tensions
excerpt:
More than 13,000 troops and dozens of ships, submarines and aircraft take part in Russian naval drills across the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Northwest Pacific. (Credit: East2West)

Japan scrambl...
body_text:
More than 13,000 troops and dozens of ships, submarines and aircraft take part in Russian naval drills across the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Northwest Pacific. (Credit: East2West)

Japan scrambled fighter jets early Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace, prompting a rapid military response ahead of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's warning of rising global instability during the Quad Leaders’ Summit in Manila.

Hours later, President Donald Trump had also joined Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the summit, where the leaders voiced opposition to actions threatening regional peace and stability.

"We strongly oppose any destabilizing or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability," the leaders said in a joint statement later released by the White House.

TRUMP KICKS OFF HIGH-STAKES ASIA TRIP WITH XI, PUTIN MEETINGS LOOMING ON WORLD STAGE

Japan scrambled fighter jets after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace, prompting a rapid military response. (Aviation-images.com/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

On Wednesday, two U.S. military officials confirmed to Fox News that the aircraft carrier USS George Washington was departing the Middle East for the Pacific.

Sen. Mazie Hirono, D-Hawaii, questioned acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao Tuesday about the lack of aircraft carriers in the Pacific, noting that three carrier strike groups had been deployed to the Middle East.

"There are none in the Indo-Pacific area when we are looking at China, not to mention North Korea and especially what China may have in mind," Hirono said.

"See, this is stretching and stressing our resources. You can't take away the strike group out of the Indo-Pacific."

The Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace northwest of Okinoshima, an island in southwestern Japan's Fukuoka Prefecture, at about 4:07 a.m. local time Nov. 17, according to Japan's Defense Ministry.

Fighter jets from the Japan Air Self-Defense Force's Western Air Defense Force were scrambled to issue warnings and take other measures, the ministry said in a statement posted on X.

The first suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace at approximately 4:07 a.m. and remained for three minutes.

A second aircraft entered the same area at approximately 4:09 a.m. and departed three minutes later.

THREE MANILA MOMENTS THAT GIVE TRUMP MOMENTUM GOING INTO TALKS WITH CHINA

U.S. President Donald Trump, second from right, poses for photos with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, left; Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, second left; and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as they take part in a meeting of the Quad group at the Solaire Resort on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit in Manila Nov. 17, 2026. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

Japan's Defense Ministry said the aircraft traveled through the Tsushima Strait and passed between Japan's Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before continuing into the Pacific Ocean.

"In response, the Self-Defense Forces scrambled fighter jets from the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s Western Air Defense Force to issue notifications and warnings and take other measures," the Ministry of Defense said.

Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Tokyo lodged a strong protest with Moscow and demanded measures to prevent further airspace violations.

The incidents "not only constitute a grave infringement upon Japan’s sovereignty but also pose a threat to our security. They are entirely unacceptable," Koizumi said.

This came as Takaichi warned of growing instability in the international order and promised a bigger role for Japan in maintaining regional security.

CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks during a news conference at the prime minister's office in Tokyo Oct. 21, 2025. (Eugene Hoshiko)

"While the international order is experiencing a period of great instability, Japan will play a more proactive role," Takaichi said during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila.

Takaichi emphasized Japan's commitment to maintaining an international order based on freedom, openness and the rule of law while strengthening cooperation with Southeast Asian nations.

"Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific," Trump had also said ahead of the Quad meeting.

The leaders had expressed "grave concerns" about economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions, and outlined plans for a joint military exercise involving maritime patrol aircraft in 2027.

KIM JONG UN'S NUCLEAR BUILDUP SPARKS 'SERIOUS CONCERN' AHEAD OF TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT

An F-35C stealth jet sits on the deck of the USS Carl Vinson in the Western Pacific, south of Japan. (Reuters/Tim Kelly)

The airspace incursion comes amid broader security concerns across the Indo-Pacific, where Japan and its regional partners have increasingly monitored Russian and Chinese military activity.

On Tuesday, South Korea’s air force also scrambled fighter jets as multiple Russian military aircraft had entered the country’s air defense identification zone, according to the Ministry of National Defense.

Otherwise, Japan's relations with Moscow have deteriorated since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, with Tokyo joining Western allies in imposing sanctions on the Kremlin.

The two countries are also locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over islands north of Japan's northernmost main island of Hokkaido. Russia administers the islands, which Japan claims as its Northern Territories.

Japan previously scrambled fighter jets in 2024 after a Russian military patrol aircraft entered Japanese airspace near Hokkaido three times.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Elon Musk claims ‘I’m not Maga’ and says he regrets vast sums to back Republicans
excerpt:
Musk, who aligned with Trump and was frequent White House guest, says he feels ‘pretty foolish’ about record midterm spending

Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intens...
body_text:
Musk, who aligned with Trump and was frequent White House guest, says he feels ‘pretty foolish’ about record midterm spending

Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intensely with Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement since 2024.

“I’m not Maga,” the world’s richest person told the New York Times Dealbook summit, which he attended via video call from China, where he is one of several US business leaders who have accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia.

“I’m not sure what Maga means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that,” the chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla added.

Musk famously declared at a 2024 campaign rally in Madison Square Garden: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.”

In a 45-minute interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin, a New York Times columnist, Musk also said it would be good for Washington to have split control between the two parties, and that he thinks “there are positives and negatives in both”.

He also accused Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, of “lying” about restrictions on access to his firm’s Starshield satellite system; praised Jensen Huang, the ousted Nvidia chief executive; and said that “no one I met at Anthropic set off my evil detector”.

Asked about his previous negative comments about Anthropic, Musk said that before he agreed to rent computing power to the AI firm: “I went to met with a lot of people at Anthropic. I didn’t just move forward with the deal.”

“My interaction so far with the Anthropic team is that they seem like good people and they seem principled,” Musk added. “They seem diligent and they seem seem to care about the future.”

Musk donated at least $250m of his own money to help Trump win the election in 2024, and recently spent nearly $500m in the US midterms to support Republicans, many of whom lost.

Musk admitted at the Dealbook summit that his spending had “failed”, and that he felt “pretty foolish” for spending such a sum, the most that anyone has ever spent in a political cycle when they themselves did not run for office. “It certainly shows that American elections are not just about money,” he said. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

After Trump took office for the second time in 2025, Musk served for 180 days heading the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) within Trump’s administration, before stepping down following a very public falling out with the president.

That culminated in Musk posting on his social media platform in June of that year: “Time to drop the really big bomb: @realDonaldTrump is in the Epstein files. That is the real reason they have not been made public.”

The two men later reconciled. During his time leading Doge, Musk frequently appeared in the Oval Office and at cabinet meetings alongside the president, often sporting hats that read “Make America Great Again” or “Trump was right about everything”.

title: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
excerpt:
Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack

The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.

The Moscow-...
body_text:
Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack

The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting mainland Russia to occupied Crimea.

The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.

The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November

It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.

Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.

At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".

President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine

Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.

That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.

In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.

Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.

Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded

BBC reports from Kyiv bridge hit by Russian attack

title: Record-breaking rain lashes California’s Bay area as ‘atmospheric river’ arrives
excerpt:
Storm expected to move into southern California, with LA residents warned of potential evacuation orders

Heavy rain pounded California’s Bay area, with record rainfall in downtown San Francisco and f...
body_text:
Storm expected to move into southern California, with LA residents warned of potential evacuation orders

Heavy rain pounded California’s Bay area, with record rainfall in downtown San Francisco and flooding and power outages across the region, as an “atmospheric river” arrived on Wednesday and dumped precipitation across the state.

The storm was expected to move into southern California on Wednesday night and Thursday, with Los Angeles warning residents in mudslide-prone areas of potential evacuation orders to come. Southern Californians were also warned of potential coastal flooding, heavy surf, wave damage to coastal piers and parking lots and beach sand erosion. Heavy snow warnings were issued for higher elevations of the Sierra Mountains, including in the Greater Lake Tahoe area.

Downtown San Francisco saw the most rainfall before noon in 76 years, at 2.11in, surpassing a record from 1950, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. By 3pm, Wednesday’s daily total of 2.28in had broken the record for the most rainfall on 18 November, which was previously set in 1918, the National Weather Service reported. South of San Francisco, in Santa Clara, there was flooding and standing water on several highways.

In San Jose, the local fire department posted on social media that two vehicles with passengers inside had become stranded in the flooded streets downtown near the SAP Center, the city’s major events arena. The second passenger was being extricated via a boat rescue, the department wrote.

Daniel Lurie, the San Francisco mayor, warned city residents the region’s winter storm and flood season, supercharged by this year’s very strong El Niño weather, was just getting started.

Despite the Wednesday afternoon break in the rain, he posted on social media, “The storm should pick back up tonight, and more rain is in the forecast for next week.”

“When these heavy storms come, we expect flooding to return to many of the same areas that were impacted this morning,” he added.

“Today’s storm certainly gave the Bay Area a good assessment of our pain points for future storms this season,” Drew Tuma, a local meteorologist for ABC7 News, wrote on social media.

Street flooding in San Francisco left maintenance hole covers floating in one neighborhood of San Francisco, while the self-driving car company Waymo temporarily suspended service in the city, the Chronicle reported. One Waymo stalled in a flooded street and blocked traffic, ABC7 News reported.

An overwhelmed sewer stormwater system also appeared to result in several “sewage geysers”, one reportedly 15-ft tall, the Chronicle reported, sharing bystander footage of the spew in the city’s Ocean Beach neighborhood.

Thousands across the Bay area were dealing with storm-related power outages by Wednesday afternoon, according to a customer outage map from Pacific Gas & Electric, the major utility company for much of northern California.

In Monterey, south of San Francisco, the local aquarium posted on social media that “storms and massive waves are causing a surge of sea otter strandings this week in Monterey Bay” and that their staff “safely rescued several pups” after receiving calls from local community members.

Areas of the state still recovering from recent wildfires continue to be at risk for flash flooding, with specific warnings issued for “burn scar” areas including in Big Sur and the Napa valley.

In Los Angeles, city officials warned residents of areas burned by the 2025 Palisades, Sunset and Hurst fires, north of the city, to be prepared for potential evacuation orders starting on Wednesday night, as heavy rains brought increased risk of flooding, mudslide and debris flow.

Statewide, the heaviest of the rainfall was expected north-east of San Francisco, from Santa Rosa to Chico and Redding in the state’s Central valley, and in the southern part of the Bay Area, along coastal mountain ranges from Santa Cruz to San Jose and Palo Alto, according to the National Weather Service.

“Travel delays, localized flooding and hazardous conditions are possible, especially along the coast and on mountain pass roads,” AccuWeather warned in an online forecast.

Atmospheric rivers, massive currents of water vapor that can carry as much or even more water than an actual river, have been growing stronger and deadlier in recent years. In the relatively dry western US, atmospheric river storms provide both essential precipitation and flood risk.

In southern California, the NWS predicted 1-3in of rain in many areas, with 3in-5in in some mountain and foothill areas, and a 20% chance of thunderstorms on Wednesday and Thursday. As much as a foot of snow was expected in higher-elevation areas above 6,000ft. There was a high risk of “significant road flooding” and a moderate risk for rockslides and mudslides, the NWS said.

The risk of coastal wave damage was expected to peak in southern California on Thursday, with additional risks expected next week, with seasonal high tides overlapping with storm risks during Thanksgiving week.

Waterspouts were spotted over the San Francisco Bay earlier this week, and the NWS flagged the risk of additional waterspouts over the ocean east of San Francisco on Wednesday.

title: Obama-era homeless policy fueled crisis it promised to end, expert says as Trump admin makes striking reversal
excerpt:
In an interview with Fox News Digital, homeless services veteran Michele Steeb says rising homelessness despite increased spending exposes deep flaws in the Housing First approach.

The Trump administ...
body_text:
In an interview with Fox News Digital, homeless services veteran Michele Steeb says rising homelessness despite increased spending exposes deep flaws in the Housing First approach.

The Trump administration’s decision to permanently cut federal funding to Los Angeles’ scandal-plagued homeless agency marks a stunning reversal of an Obama-era policy that one expert said produced massive failures.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, homeless services veteran Michele Steeb broke down Tuesday’s announcement from the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) that it is severing ties with the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA).

Steeb said the Housing First model adopted by LAHSA, which provides housing unconditionally without requiring individuals to pursue sobriety or mental health treatment, was championed by former President Barack Obama.

HUD’S HOMELESSNESS REFORMS PUT HUMAN LIVES AHEAD OF HOUSING BUREAUCRACYShe argued the model discouraged recovery by allowing people to remain in subsidized housing indefinitely, leaving fewer available units for others seeking permanent housing.

"So, back in 2013, when they instituted this, President Obama promised that this very different approach would end homelessness in a decade. And a decade later, we were at an almost 35% increase with no accountability," Steeb said, referring to the national homeless population.

Former President Barack Obama championed Housing First, an approach Michele Steeb argues failed to deliver on its promise to end homelessness. (Getty Images/File)

The program ultimately "eliminates purpose from individuals," Steeb said. "They're given housing for life without any requirements."

Earlier this year, Obama called Los Angeles' homelessness crisis a moral "atrocity," arguing that homelessness programs must pair assistance with accountability.

"We should recognize that the average person doesn’t want to have to navigate around a tent city in the middle of downtown," Obama said. "That’s a losing political strategy."

EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE LA'S HOMELESS HELLSCAPE — UNLIKELY CRITICS BLAST DEMS AS GOP HOPEFUL TOURS SKID ROW

California, which adopted the model statewide, offers a particularly striking example of what Steeb views as its shortcomings. Despite significant government investment, homelessness has continued to climb rather than move toward the promised goal of ending it.

Steeb said homelessness in California surged 40% between 2016 and 2025, even as federal spending on homelessness increased at least 200% under the Housing First approach instituted in 2013.

The situation has been particularly stark in Los Angeles, where homelessness climbed between 60% and 70% over the past five years despite LAHSA receiving more than $1 billion in federal funding.

Homelessness climbed despite billions in spending, fueling calls from expert Michele Steeb for greater accountability and treatment requirements. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images/File)

LA HOMELESSNESS FRAUD CASES EXPOSE DEEPER PROBLEM THAN STOLEN MILLIONS, OVERSIGHT HAWK WARNS

Steeb said, despite the mounting evidence of failure, defenders of the system continued to blame the homelessness crisis on insufficient funding.

"It's a shame to me that the system, what I often call the homeless industrial complex, is trying to defend it," she said.

"It just has failed so massively. So, there's no excuses except that it was the wrong approach."

Los Angeles County will take over the embattled homeless agency’s responsibilities, though Michele Steeb questions how much the transition will improve services. (Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images/File)

Steeb said HUD's settlement represents an effort by the Trump administration to restore accountability to homeless services after LAHSA became embroiled in allegations of fraud and financial mismanagement.

The agency's funding will soon be transferred to Los Angeles County, according to officials.

Although Steeb acknowledged the county has its own problems, she hopes the transition could improve a system she believes has failed to address the crisis.

"I'm hopeful. … I think it's better than LAHSA, but I don't think it's going to be that much better," Steeb said.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Beau Lamarre-Condon’s testimony about Jesse Baird and Luke Davies’ deaths ‘fanciful in the extreme’, crown alleges
excerpt:
Prosecutor argues accused could be convicted on strength of forensic and ballistics evidence alone in closing statement

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condo...
body_text:
Prosecutor argues accused could be convicted on strength of forensic and ballistics evidence alone in closing statement

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon’s claims about the deaths of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies are “fanciful in the extreme”, a court has heard.

The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

The crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC began delivering his closing statement on Thursday as the double murder trial entered its ninth week.

The defence had argued the two men died in struggles with the accused when he acted in “self-defence”.

Lamarre-Condon had previously told the court he was aiming to shoot Baird in the shoulder to get him to drop a knife, and accidentally shot him a second time as they fell to the ground.

But Hatfield told the court the injury from the first shot would cause someone to pass out.

“Common sense renders it completely improbable that you could suffer such an injury yet immediately grab hold of a pistol with your left and forcefully pull a person brandishing it to the ground,” Hatfield said.

“Such a scenario, you might think, is fanciful in the extreme.”

He argued Lamarre-Condon could be convicted on the strength of the forensic and ballistics evidence alone.

Forensic evidence of the directionality of the bullet and the wounds on Baird’s body indicated Lamarre-Condon shot Baird in the back as the other man fled towards the back door, Hatfield alleged.

The height of the bullet marks meant Baird must have been ducking or stooping at the time, according to the prosecution.

Hatfield said the near-vertical trajectory of the bullet through the floor spoke to a controlled shot through Baird’s temple, with the prosecutor calling it an “execution-style shot”.

The timing between the two shots allowed only for a quick two to three steps, the crown prosecutor told the court.

“Not the bizarre wrestling and yanking the accused has described,” Hatfield said.

At this point, Davies must have realised something was “seriously amiss”, the prosecutor said, and attempted to call triple zero.

There was no doubt he was then killed by a bullet that passed through the door and into his head, Hatfield said, telling the court there was gunshot stippling on the door but not the body.

Aspects of the defence’s case, that Baird lunged at Lamarre-Condon with a knife and that Davies picked up the gun and pointed it at the accused, came only from the former officer himself, Hatfield said.

“Nothing independent of him supports any of what he said about those events,” Hatfield told the jury.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

title: No 1 Florida loses to Houston as four of the preseason AP top five fall before Thanksgiving
excerpt:
"This was the worst offseason in the history of college basketball. Because of the chaos. There's no question about it. "

Houston had waited since April 2025 for another shot at Florida. On Wednesday...
body_text:
"This was the worst offseason in the history of college basketball. Because of the chaos. There's no question about it. "

Houston had waited since April 2025 for another shot at Florida. On Wednesday, the Cougars made sure this one would not be decided in the final minute.

No. 8 Houston beat No. 1 Florida 86-76 in Las Vegas, advancing to the Players Era 8 championship game and handing the Gators their first loss of the season. Florida had beaten Houston 65-63 in the 2025 national championship game. Florida’s loss also means four of the preseason AP top five have already been beaten, with Duke losing twice.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Houston Cougars players celebrate against the Florida Gators during the 2026 Players Era Men's Championship at Michelob ULTRA Arena. (Getty Images)

Florida, which was the AP preseason No. 1 and entered the game 5-0, led 40-37 at halftime. Houston took the lead early in the second half before Florida briefly regained the lead at 47-46. But Houston scored the next 11 points and never trailed again, building a lead as large as 14 points.

Dedan Thomas Jr. scored 30 for the Cougars, while Joseph Tugler recorded a 12-point, 10-rebound double-double.

KENTUCKY NEEDS BUZZER-BEATING THREE TO SURVIVE NORTHERN ARIZONA'S UPSET BID AT RUPP ARENA

Kelvin Sampson’s Houston program entered the game ranked eighth and has been among the sport’s contenders for years. Still, beating the team that denied Houston a national title, and doing it while that team sat at No. 1, gives the Cougars a massive November resume boost.

It also makes the analytics look pretty smart. The AP voters had Houston 10th in the preseason, but KenPom rated the Cougars third. After beating Florida by 10 on a neutral floor, Houston looks a lot closer to No. 3 than No. 10.

Florida joins Duke, Illinois and Arizona as preseason AP top five teams that have already lost less than three weeks into the college basketball season. UConn is the lone unbeaten member of that group, at least heading into its Wednesday night visit to Arizona.

Thomas Haugh, who played on Florida’s 2025 national championship team, scored 18 points in Wednesday’s loss to Houston. (Getty Images)

Arizona was the first to fall, losing 84-75 to UCLA on opening night. The Wildcats are ranked No. 12 in this week's poll. A week later, Michigan State beat then-No. 2 Duke 79-73, while Texas Tech knocked off then-No. 3 Illinois 84-78.

Illinois responded Tuesday by going into Duke and winning by 21. The Blue Devils, the preseason No. 2, have now lost twice before Thanksgiving. The Michigan State loss only dropped Duke from No. 2 to No. 5, but expect another fall for the Blue Devils when the Week 4 rankings come out on Nov. 23.

Michigan State’s stay at No. 2 may be short, too. After beating Duke, the Spartans managed just 46 points in a 61-46 loss at No. 14 Tennessee on Tuesday.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

And the trouble has reached beyond the preseason favorites. Unranked Memphis opened its season by beating No. 18 Iowa State 80-76. The Tigers followed that by erasing an 18-point deficit against No. 10 Louisville on Sunday and winning 98-78 after outscoring Louisville by 31 points in the second half.

Joseph Tugler and the No. 8 Houston Cougars upset the No. 1 Florida Gators on Wednesday. (Getty Images)

Over the weekend, LSU went to Gonzaga and beat the then-No. 14 Bulldogs 81-80 on a late shot. On Tuesday, Indiana added an 81-76 win over No. 20 Arkansas.

Kentucky can be grateful it is missing from that list. The Wildcats, who entered the game as 30-point favorites, needed a late three-pointer to escape Northern Arizona 78-77 at Rupp Arena last week, a close call that fit the season’s mood even if it didn't count as another upset.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

None of this settles who will matter in March because there is still a lot of basketball to play. I'm certainly not ready to write off Florida, Duke, Arizona or Illinois because of an early-season hiccup (or two, in Duke's case).

Still, that’s five losses for the preseason AP top five. The voters put Florida first and Michigan State second on Monday. By Wednesday night, both had lost by double digits. Good luck with next Monday’s ballot (If the AP has a spare one, I’ll take it).

title: Tyler Herro's three-words sums up status with ex-teammate Bam Adebayo for first game since punching incident

body_text:
Colin Cowherd discusses Bam Adebayo’s 83-point explosion against the Washington Wizards, and asks how this game will be remembered.

The Miami Heat welcomed the Milwaukee Bucks on Wednesday night in a matchup that might otherwise blend into the early-season NBA schedule.

But a summer feud involving a former Heat player and one of Miami’s current stars has added an unexpected layer of intrigue to the matchup. In July, tensions between Bam Adebayo and Tyler Herro reportedly boiled over in Las Vegas.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Since the dispute between the two NBA stars, questions have lingered over whether Bam Adebayo and Tyler Herro had repaired their relationship or whether tensions remained.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Bam Adebayo and Tyler Herro of the Miami Heat exit the court during a delay in a game against the Chicago Bulls at the United Center in Chicago, Illinois, on Jan. 8, 2026. (Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Wednesday marked the first time the two players faced each other since the incident, and Herro was noncommittal when asked about the state of their relationship.

HEAT VS. BUCKS BEST BETS: GIANNIS GETS HIS FIRST SHOT AT MILWAUKEE

"I'm not sure. I haven't talked to him," Herro told reporters Wednesday.

Adebayo and Herro were involved in a physical altercation at an NBA Summer League practice facility, during which the Heat center allegedly struck the Milwaukee Bucks guard in the head area.

A blockbuster deal over this past offseason sent Giannis Antetokounmpo to Miami and Herro to Milwaukee, ending his time as Adebayo’s Heat teammate.

Bam Adebayo and Tyler Herro react during the fourth quarter against the Atlanta Hawks at Kaseya Center on March 27, 2025, in Miami, Florida. (Getty Images)

MIAMI HEAT UNVEIL VICE CITY COURT FOR 'GRAND THEFT AUTO VI'-THEMED CLASH WITH MILWAUKEE BUCKS

Herro reflected on his time sharing a locker room with Adebayo, and praised the three-time All-Star's skillset. "Obviously I spent a lot of time with Bam. I admire his game. He's a great player. Can do everything on the floor, guard 1-5. He's gifted offensively."

Sources told ESPN that Adebayo initially confronted Herro over alleged social media comments criticizing his defense. Screenshots circulated online purportedly showed Herro questioning Adebayo’s defensive prowess in an Instagram direct message with a fan.

Milwaukee Bucks guard Tyler Herro drives against Atlanta Hawks guard RayJ Dennis in the first half at Fiserv Forum in Milwaukee, Wis., on Nov. 15, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Adebayo agreed to a three-year, $166 million extension with Miami in June 2024. The alleged DM also appeared to question whether his nightly defensive effort justified a salary approaching $60 million.

Miami entered Wednesday night with an 8-6 record, while Milwaukee had won just once this season.
