title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
excerpt:
Watch: Inside the gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia

There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces h...
body_text:
Watch: Inside the gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia

There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.

"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.

Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.

The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.

But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.

Troops move through the tunnel on special sleds - they call it the Kupyansk metro

A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.

They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.

Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.

Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."

Ukrainian troops like Musician rarely see the sun - but they say they feel safer underground

The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.

There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.

"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.

But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.

It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.

Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.

The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.

The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."

His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."

The men live and fight in very tight quarters - but have managed to clear 15km of the pipe

Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.

From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.

Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.

Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.

Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.

"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."

Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.

While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.

But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."

In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.

It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success.

It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale, but on its own it has not changed the course of the war.

Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

title: Kuwait, Bahrain face new Iran attacks after US strike on Qeshm Island
excerpt: Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Isl...
body_text:
Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Island.

Kuwait said it activated its air defences to counter drone strikes – the first since early September – and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack early on Wednesday, a day after the US attacked a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

The US said it carried out the strike in response to an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain earlier on Tuesday.

Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, has experienced four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.

Iran said its recent attacks were in response to US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.

The uptick in fighting raises the risk of a wider escalation towards the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.

The Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries have drawn condemnation from across the region.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Iranian attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain “in the strongest terms” and denounced an attack on a tanker belonging to the United Arab Emirates.

The ministry said the kingdom rejects Iran’s disruption of shipping routes and urged a negotiated solution.

Arab League chief Nabil Fahmy said the repeated attacks on Arab countries reveal “a continuous escalation pattern that threatens to widen the circle of confrontation”. He also condemned the targeting of a ship belonging to the UAE’s national oil company, ADNOC, as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz.

Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, the Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, held Iran “responsible for this escalation and its repercussions on regional security”.

Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the attacks “a dangerous escalation” that risks undermining diplomatic efforts. Kuwait and the UAE also condemned them.

Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry described the drone attacks as flagrant violations of its sovereignty and a direct threat to its security, Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi reported from Doha.

Basravi also said Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, warned that continued escalation without restraint from both the US and Iran makes a negotiated solution, or even continued dialogue, harder.

Meanwhile, Iran’s army chief, Major-General Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were “monitoring the enemy’s movements” after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East, the Fars news agency reported.

He said Iran’s response to any misstep by the US and its “backers” would be “even more crushing”.

title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
excerpt:
Kuwait condemned the attack, which Iran said targeted an airbase hosting US forces (file photo)

Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran an...
body_text:
Kuwait condemned the attack, which Iran said targeted an airbase hosting US forces (file photo)

Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.

The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.

It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.

The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.

The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.

Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump

Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington

Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack

On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.

The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".

"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.

Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".

The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.

Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".

The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.

Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.

"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.

On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.

Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.

In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.

Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".

At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Tyler Robinson defense wants testing on bullet fragments paused in assassination of Charlie Kirk
excerpt:
Finn reports on the upcoming court proceedings, the timeline leading up to the trial and the latest developments in the high-profile case surrounding Kirk's assassination.

Attorneys for Charlie Kirk'...
body_text:
Finn reports on the upcoming court proceedings, the timeline leading up to the trial and the latest developments in the high-profile case surrounding Kirk's assassination.

Attorneys for Charlie Kirk's accused assassin Tyler Robinson are asking a Utah judge to put additional ballistics testing on pause as prosecutors attempt to conclusively link bullet fragments recovered at autopsy to the suspected murder weapon, which some experts call unnecessary and even prosecutors admit isn't central to their case.

The Utah County Attorney's Office has asked the judge to deny the motion, countering that the testing they are seeking will not consume the evidence or prevent Robinson's experts from having a look at it once the government is done — and that they have more compelling evidence to introduce at trial.

"There is no reason to believe the bullet fragments contain exculpatory evidence," Deputy Utah County Attorney Ryan McBride alleged in an opposition to the defense motion. "To the contrary, all the evidence points to the inculpatory value of the fragments."

TYLER ROBINSON JUDGE UNSEALS ATF REPORT IN ASSASSINATION OF CHARLIE KIRK

Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, listens during a preliminary hearing at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

Robinson has allegedly admitted to the shooting, he wrote. Three unspent cartridges in the rifle were consistent with the gunshot fired at Kirk. The bullet fragments were consistent with the suspected murder weapon, although they have not been conclusively identified to it. And police recovered video evidence and a Dremel tool consistent with etchings made on brass casings recovered in the rifle at the scene.

While the fragment testing, known as virtual comparison microscopy (VCM), won't destroy the evidence, it is expected to physically alter or even damage it, according to court filings. "Petals" from the fragments may be folded out of the way as investigators look for rifling markings on the underlying surface, according to prosecutors. The fragments may be cleaned, at least in a small area. And lead fragments may be cleaned or scraped. There is a risk that pieces break off during the process.

TYLER ROBINSON'S DEFENSE TEAM FIGHTS TO SEAL EVIDENCE AND PUNISH PROSECUTORS IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION

Bullet fragments are shown on a screen during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

Robinson's lawyers want the VCM testing placed on hold until they have a chance to examine and photograph the same evidence — or an order allowing a defense expert to observe the testing in person or via a video recording, something the FBI does not allow for a number of reasons, including contamination and national security concerns.

They argued that prior ATF testing already damaged the evidence, and the next round of testing could result in further harm.

CHARLIE KIRK JUDGE DENIES TYLER ROBINSON'S ATTEMPT TO HAVE POTENTIAL DEATH PENALTY REMOVED

Samantha Karner, a firearm and tool mark examiner for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, holds a model of a bullet while she testifies during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

"The ATF couldn’t conclusively connect the bullet fragment to the recovered rifle, but it couldn’t rule out the rifle either," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory agent who has been following the case. "That’s an important distinction, and it helps explain why prosecutors want the FBI to take another look."

He explained that VCM is a more advanced process than simply looking at the fragments under a microscope, a more traditional method. Even so, there's no guarantee that examiners will find a more conclusive link between the fragments and the suspected murder weapon.

CHARLIE KIRK'S FAMILY COMES FACE TO FACE WITH ACCUSED ASSASSIN FOR FIRST TIME

"If the markings are too damaged or simply aren’t there anymore, even the best technology can’t bring them back," Pack told Fox News Digital.

Robinson is accused of shooting Kirk at Utah Valley University during a Turning Point USA public speaking event on Sept. 10, 2025. During Kirk's autopsy, investigators recovered a bullet jacket fragment and four lead fragments from his body, according to prosecutors.

An image that shows ammunition, including a casing engraved with the words "TEST SHOT" is displayed during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION

"If the bullet fragment is again altered to the point where no independent comparison is possible, then the degree of prejudice to the defendant is severe," Robinson's lawyers wrote to the court. "The defense will be unable to independently verify conclusions, cross-examination will be unfairly limited, and the jury will hear unchallengeable expert testimony."

Bernard Zapor, a former ATF special agent in charge and faculty associate at Arizona State University, said those concerns may be overblown. The fragments were already documented meticulously during the ATF's initial examination, he said, with photographs, data and images available to the defense through discovery. If the fragments are damaged during additional testing, it may not change much, since the initial testing was inconclusive — which he said is not unusual in shootings involving similar caliber weapons.

TYLER ROBINSON HEARING ENDS WITHOUT RULING AS EVIDENCE DISMANTLES CHARLIE KIRK CONSPIRACY CLAIMS

Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

"This is all distracting from the purpose of getting information to the jury so they can come to a conclusion, one way or the other," he told Fox News Digital. "This case is solid. You don’t want to do anything to disrupt it."

Robinson's lawyers previously flagged in court that they intend to challenge the ATF's findings and methodology.

During prior testing, ATF examiner Samantha Karner cleaned the jacket fragment, photographed it and then peeled the "petals" back to examine groove impressions on it. She identified the fragment as having been in the .30 caliber class, but she was unable to conclusively link it to the suspected murder weapon, Robinson's grandfather's .30-06 Mauser rifle.

TYLER ROBINSON'S AND LANCE TWIGGS' DNA BOTH ALLEGEDLY FOUND ON KEY EVIDENCE IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION

"Given the limited detail that Ms. Karner observed, she could not include or exclude the fragment as having been fired from the recovered rifle," prosecutors wrote. "She testified that there was 'no further testing that [she] could do' to try to reach a conclusive result ... However, she noted 'the possibility of using a 3D system to visualize the individual characteristics on the bullet,' to obtain more conclusive results."

People run after shots were fired during an appearance by Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

For that kind of analysis, however, the fragments would need to be sent to the FBI for VCM.

TYLER ROBINSON TO FACE TRIAL IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION AS JUDGE KEEPS DEATH PENALTY ON TABLE

"This analysis is non-destructive and uses 3D technology to capture multiple scans of the object," prosecutors wrote. "The scan data will be preserved and provided to the defense for their own analysis."

In order to perform the scans, however, analysts may have to clean the fragments or fold back warped metal, called "petals," to expose the surface of the fragment that contacted the rifle when fired, prosecutors wrote.

Tyler Robinson, accused of the murder of Charlie Kirk, appears during a hearing in Fourth District Court in Provo, Utah, on Thursday, Dec. 11, 2025. (Rick Egan/The Salt Lake Tribune via Pool)

TYLER ROBINSON PROSECUTORS: NO DNA, NO PROBLEM — PILE OF EVIDENCE TO PUSH CHARLIE KIRK CASE TOWARD JUSTICE

Prosecutors are also seeking another type of testing, known as metallurgical testing, on the bullet jacket fragment and at least one piece of lead, according to court filings. That testing might require cleaning "around a small area," prosecutors added, before it is examined with an X-ray.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"The FBI is also proposing separate testing to compare the metal in the recovered bullet fragments with ammunition seized during the investigation," Pack said. "That could provide additional information, although it wouldn’t conclusively identify the firearm."

Lastly, prosecutors want an examiner to disassemble one of the unfired .30-06 cartridges found at Robinson's home after his arrest, for comparison.

Robinson's attorneys entered not guilty pleas on his behalf to all charges. He could face the potential death penalty if convicted of the top count of aggravated murder.

title: Pakistan's solar revolution is so successful the national grid is lagging behind
excerpt:
Faizal Shahzad wants to buy several more solar panels to make his home in rural Punjab fully self-sufficient

Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after h...
body_text:
Faizal Shahzad wants to buy several more solar panels to make his home in rural Punjab fully self-sufficient

Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.

But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.

"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."

Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.

From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.

People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."

Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.

This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.

The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.

Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".

"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."

While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.

Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.

When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.

Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.

"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.

More and more households are installing solar panels, as seen here in Karachi, but Pakistanis still need energy from the national grid

Pakistan's government says the costs are already being felt.

"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."

The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.

Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.

Leghari wants the country to run on "up to 90% clean power" by the end of 2036 - including renewables and nuclear - with dependence on imported energy reducing from 26% to 4%.

The solar power boom in Pakistan and the Philippines

Cheap solar panels, mainly imported from China, are transforming lives and slashing electricity bills across Asia.

But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.

Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.

When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.

But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy.

"We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether.

"The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."

Rows of large solar panels power this textiles factory in Islamabad for large parts of the day

Critics accuse the government of moving the goalposts on solar power. Previously, households could feed excess electricity into the grid and earn credits, which were then used to offset the cost of grid power when the sun wasn't shining. That policy changed earlier this year.

"Initially their policy was very helpful," says Arif Ehsan Malik, president of Faisalabad's chamber of commerce. "But then the policy changed. Now they have started purchasing at a lower rate and selling back at a higher rate."

Malik says that makes a big difference for small and medium businesses. Leghari counters that the costs of the initial model didn't add up; the electricity the solar producers put into the system was much cheaper than the electricity they ended up taking out of it.

"Those profits were coming at the cost of the rest of the consumers of the grid. Had we not changed those regulations, the rest of the consumers would have been burdened by at least 150 to 200 billion rupees a year, say, two years from now."

Muhammad Hassan Dajana from Renewables First believes that with the right policy, Pakistan could become a global example of a successful energy transition

Despite admitting that the first wave of solar adoption was a "surprise" to the government, Leghari says he has no fear that solar could outrun their plans, saying it has been incorporated into their 10-year forecasts and the numbers leaving the grid have slowed.

Pakistan has big ambitions for solar; there are plans to open solar battery factories around the country and encourage more electric vehicles.

"There are two paths ahead," Dajana says. One is a future where solar and the grid work in parallel, demonstrating how a gradual energy transition can succeed. The other is where Pakistan becomes a cautionary tale, burdened with a costly, declining grid.

Shahzad's solar ambitions for his home in rural Punjab certainly have not slowed.

"We plan to get another 10-15 panels and install them on the roof, then connect a full system with batteries and back up.

"The plan is to be fully self-sufficient."

Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'

Devastation on repeat: How climate change is worsening Pakistan's deadly floods

Melting glaciers leave homes teetering in valley of jagged mountains

title: MIKE DAVIS: Washington is strangling the humble radio
excerpt:
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr joined ‘Pod Force One’ to discuss the Trump administration’s push to ‘rebalance’ the media by encouraging local broadcasters to air more pro-America programming.

When tornad...
body_text:
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr joined ‘Pod Force One’ to discuss the Trump administration’s push to ‘rebalance’ the media by encouraging local broadcasters to air more pro-America programming.

When tornado sirens sound, high school and college basketball games tip off or farmers need the latest crop and weather report, Americans still turn to local radio. Yet Washington keeps imposing last-century rules on the stations that provide it. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr now has a chance to deliver real reform, not for a favored industry but for the communities that depend on radio.

Congress set these ownership caps in 1996. This was when dial-up internet was cutting-edge, CDs were king, the iPod did not exist, and satellite radio had not yet launched.

CDs are dead. The iPod is gone. A hometown station now battles Spotify, SiriusXM, YouTube, podcasts, social media and the largest technology companies on earth. Those national giants reach nearly every American with a smartphone, and no federal rule caps their presence in any single town.

Brendan Carr, commissioner at the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), during a Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee oversight hearing in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Dec. 17, 2025. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

DAVID MARCUS: CONGRESS SET TO PROTECT AM RADIO AND AMERICAN DISCOURSE

The station down the road — warning where the storm is headed, carrying the high school game and reporting livestock and grain prices — faces tighter federal limits under rules from a bygone era.

Carr is right to call this regulatory nostalgia. The question is simple: Will Washington let small stations build the scale to survive, or protect bureaucratic boxes while listeners lose the service they count on?

STEVE FORBES: REGULATORS RISK DESTROYING LOCAL TV BY BLOCKING KEY MEDIA MERGER

The current framework uses a sliding scale. Even in the largest markets, one company generally may own no more than eight stations and no more than five in either AM or FM. Smaller markets face stricter caps still.

The rule pretends radio lives in a sealed-off world that online platforms and endless digital choices never touch. Today's FCC should recognize those Big Tech competitors and scrap this relic.

Nobody in the school pickup line or tractor cab cares about federal categories. They choose between a local morning show, a podcast, satellite radio and a streaming playlist, often within the same commute. That is one marketplace, and every competitor in it fights for the same listeners and advertising dollars.

Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr speaks at a news conference following an FCC meeting in Washington, D.C on Feb. 18, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

CARS FLIPPED, SCHOOL DEVASTATED AS VIOLENT TWISTER RIPS THROUGH POPULAR CITY

These caps threaten the local service they claim to protect. Newsrooms, towers, backup generators, engineers and on-air talent cost serious money, and a standalone station often cannot shoulder that burden by itself. Sharing those costs across stations can keep emergency alerts live, ballgames on the dial and agricultural reports reaching the people who need them. Deny that scale, and Washington risks shutting down a vital source of news for rural and small-town America.

When twisters strike, floods rise, wildfires spread or cellular networks fail, free over-the-air radio becomes the lifeline. If the power goes out, a battery-powered receiver still works when nothing else does. Broadcasters on the ground know the roads, schools, shelters and hospitals. Obsolete rules should not push those voices toward silence.

Flooded road conditions are seen as emergency crews respond to multiple storm-related calls across Texas. (White Settlement Police Department)

BIPARTISAN LAWMAKERS WANT TO STRIP BIG TECH'S LEGAL IMMUNITY THAT CAN SHIELD SOCIAL MEDIA COMPANIES

Critics will shout "monopoly," but they aim at the wrong target. Ending arbitrary caps would not eliminate FCC review of station purchases or block action against actual competitive harm, and the Justice Department would keep its antitrust authority over radio deals. Reform would stop the government from treating another locally operated station as more dangerous than a nationwide platform with enormous reach.

Conservatives cannot trust federal bureaucrats to manufacture "viewpoint diversity" by counting how many microphones a private company may own. Genuine diversity comes from voices with deep roots in their communities — voices that know the county fair, the homecoming rivalry, the weekend forecast and the needs of family farms and small businesses. The First Amendment is safer in the hands of listeners than regulators.

Chairman Carr should follow the evidence and eliminate local ownership caps. Let broadcasters invest, compete and keep homegrown voices on the air for another generation. Washington must stop strangling radio before another town loses its local voice, its last dependable source of information.

Michael R. Davis is the founder and president of the Article III Project.

title: Former Penn State frat brother indicted by federal grand jury in cocaine trafficking scheme
excerpt:
From FIT's fentanyl poisoning to Penn State's cocaine ring, campus drug scares reveal how organized crime networks are targeting college students, Paul Mauro warns.

The alleged leader of a cocaine-tr...
body_text:
From FIT's fentanyl poisoning to Penn State's cocaine ring, campus drug scares reveal how organized crime networks are targeting college students, Paul Mauro warns.

The alleged leader of a cocaine-trafficking ring at Penn State University has been indicted on drug distribution charges by a federal grand jury, adding to the state charges he is already facing.

Agostino Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, was a "major supplier" of cocaine to at least two separate fraternities — Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon — at the university in State College, Pennsylvania, between January 2023 and December 2024, according to federal prosecutors.

Abbatiello, a former Sigma Chi member, frequently drove to Philadelphia and New York to buy cocaine before bringing his hauls back to campus and enlisting his fellow fraternity brothers and pledges to package the drugs for resale, according to federal and state authorities.

He'd allegedly return with as much as a kilogram each time, which factors heavily into the sheer number of charges he's facing.

Agostino Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, was charged on Nov. 18, 2026, by a federal grand jury with one count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and six counts of distribution of cocaine. He is accused of leading a drug ring at Penn State from 2023 to 2024. (Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office)

PENN STATE COCAINE RING SUSPECT’S ATTORNEY WARNS OF ‘FOOLISH’ MOVE IN ALLEGED FRAT DRUG OPERATION

Abbatiello, who graduated in spring 2024, now faces one count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and six counts of distribution of cocaine; these charges could land him in prison for the rest of his life if he's convicted.

"College should be a marketplace of ideas and not illegal drugs," said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania in a statement. "Our office will continue working with the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s office, and with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and hold accountable those who profit from illegal drug activity in our communities."

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday, a Republican and former York County district attorney, announced state charges against Abbatiello and his alleged co-conspirators in August following a joint investigation. In all, 14 people were charged at the state level.

Agostino Abbatiello arrives at Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte, Pa., Sept. 2, 2026. (Kamil Krzaczynski for Fox News Digital)

PENN STATE FRAT COCAINE BUST BLOWS LID OFF WIDER STIMULANT SCOURGE HITTING COLLEGE CAMPUSES — AND BEYOND

Thomas Robinson, who Pennsylvania authorities said made regular trips to Philadelphia and New York to buy cocaine with Abbatiello, has not been indicted in federal court.

Another state defendant was Robinson's father, Paul Robinson, who state prosecutors said tried to conceal evidence in the case, including a safe containing drugs and cash.

Sunday described Abbatiello as "the top rung of the ladder for a high-level drug trafficking ring." Robinson was a "rung below that on the ladder," he added.

Agostino Abbatiello and Thomas Robinson are accused of being the main suppliers of cocaine for a massive distribution ring where 14 people were charged. (Getty Images: Rolf Vennenbernd/picture alliance; Attorney General Dave Sunday's Office)

When he announced the state charges in August, Sunday said the cocaine was sold among Penn State students, often at parties. Investigators also found that packaging the drugs was used as an initiation ritual for fraternity pledges.

"We found a pattern of events that showed cutting and bagging cocaine was for some pledges an indoctrination into the Delta Upsilon and Sigma Chi fraternities," Sunday said.

A variety of different agencies have investigated the case, including Homeland Security Investigations, the State College Police Department and a narcotics unit within the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office.

James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.
